For all $1\le i,j\le n$ one has $X_iX_j=X_jX_i$ in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, hence in
$R[S_n]$ for every commutative ring $R$; that is, the Jucys-Murphy elements
commute pairwise, and the subalgebra they generate is commutative.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $R$ be a commutative ring. In the group ring $R[S_n]$ of
the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-group-ring]]), where $(j\ k)$ denotes the
transposition of the distinct entries $j,k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **Jucys-Murphy elements** are
$$X_1:=0,\qquad X_k:=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}(j\ k)\in R[S_n]\qquad(2\le k\le n).$$
Each $X_k$ is a finite sum of group elements with coefficient $1$, so the
formula already defines an element of the integral group ring
$\mathbb Z[S_n]$, and its image under the base change
$\mathbb Z[S_n]\to R[S_n]$ is the displayed element
([[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]); for $1\le k\le m\le n$ the element
$X_k$ of $R[S_m]$, computed in the subgroup
$S_m=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,m\})\subseteq S_n$ of permutations fixing
$m+1,\dots,n$, maps to $X_k$ under the inclusion $S_m\hookrightarrow S_n$.
Equivalently $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$, where $T_k=\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}(i\ j)$ is the
sum of all transpositions in $S_k$.

Let $n\ge1$. (a) The elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ act diagonally in the Young
basis of the previous item: for every standard tableau $T$ of size $n$ and
every $k$, $X_kv_T=c_T(k)v_T$, and the joint eigenspaces are
one-dimensional, indexed by the standard tableaux. (b) A vector
$\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$ occurs as the joint eigenvalue vector
of a $v_T$, equivalently $\alpha=\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ for a standard
tableau $T$, if and only if: (1) $a_1=0$; (2) for every $q>1$ at least one of
$a_q-1,a_q+1$ occurs among $a_1,\dots,a_{q-1}$; (3) if $a_p=a_q$ with $p<q$,
then both $a_p-1$ and $a_p+1$ occur among $a_{p+1},\dots,a_{q-1}$. The
association $T\mapsto\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ is a bijection from the standard
tableaux of size $n$ onto this set.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $I_1,\ldots,I_r$ be pairwise comaximal ideals, where $r\ge1$. Then the canonical map
$$ R\longrightarrow \prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i,\qquad x\longmapsto(x+I_1,\ldots,x+I_r) $$
is surjective, its kernel is $\bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i$, and
$$ \bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i=\prod_{i=1}^r I_i. $$
Equivalently,
$$ R/\prod_{i=1}^r I_i\cong\prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i. $$

For $H\le G$, restriction forgets from $\mathbb Z[G]$ to $\mathbb Z[H]$. For a left $H$-module $M$, set $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=\mathbb Z[G]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[H]}M$ and $\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z[H]}(\mathbb Z[G],M)$, with $G$ acting on the latter by $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$.
If $H\le G$ and a left (respectively right) coset transversal is supplied, then $\mathbb Z[G]$ is free as a right (respectively left) $\mathbb Z[H]$-module on it.

Fix a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for a finite group $G$.
A **$p$-block idempotent** is a primitive central idempotent of $\mathcal O G$
or, after reduction, of $kG$.

If $e$ is such an idempotent, the corresponding **block** is the two-sided
ideal

$$B=\mathcal OGe\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=kGe.$$

The primitive central idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, so
the algebra splits as a direct product of its block summands.

For every commutative unital ring $R$ and $n\ge0$, every element of $Z(RS_n)$ is an $R$-linear combination of evaluations of integral monomial symmetric polynomials at $L_r=\sum_{a<r}(a,r)$. Conversely every symmetric polynomial evaluation is central. In particular $Z(RS_n)=R[L_1,\ldots,L_n]^{\mathrm{sym}}$, where the right side denotes evaluations of symmetric polynomials, not invariants of an action on the group algebra. No integer is inverted.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set
of $\lambda$-tabloids; for a $\lambda$-tableau $t$ write $\{t\}$ for its
tabloid ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). The
**integral tabloid module** is the free abelian group on $\Omega_\lambda$,

$$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\mathbb Z^{(\Omega_\lambda)} =\Bigl\{\sum_{T\in\Omega_\lambda}a_T\,T:\ a_T\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{only finitely many }a_T\ne0\Bigr\},$$

with the tabloids as standard $\mathbb Z$-basis
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). The left action of $S_n$ on
tabloids extends $\mathbb Z$-linearly to $M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so that
$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is a $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-module. For every $\lambda$-tableau
$t$ put

$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma \in\mathbb Z[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\, \{\gamma\cdot t\}\in M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},$$

the **integral column polytabloid**; every coefficient lies in
$\{0,1,-1\}$ ([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).
The **integral Specht lattice** is the $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-submodule

$$S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\text{the }\mathbb Z\text{-span of } \{\,e_s:\ s\text{ a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\subseteq M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}.$$

For a commutative ring $R$ let $M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ be the free
$R$-module on the tabloids and let $S^\lambda_R\subseteq M^\lambda_R$ be the
$R$-span of the polytabloids $\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)
\{\gamma\cdot t\}$, $t$ a $\lambda$-tableau. The **standard polytabloids** are
the $e_s$ with $s$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

This item records three facts. First, the standard polytabloids form a
$\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so the integral Specht lattice has
explicit finite rank. Second, for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map
$R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}
M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\cong M^\lambda_R$ is injective onto $S^\lambda_R$: the
lattice is a direct summand of the free tabloid module and is compatible with
base change, including rings of prime characteristic. Third, for
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the module has rank one and is generated by the empty
polytabloid.

Let $G$ be a finite group and let $k$ be an algebraically closed field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$. Then there are positive integers
$n_1,\ldots,n_r$ such that

$$ k[G]\cong\prod_{i=1}^r M_{n_i}(k) $$

as $k$-algebras.

derivations.claim: *Eigenvalues in $\mathbb F_p$.* Let $h_r\in\mathbb Q[X]$ be the minimal polynomial of $L_r$ acting on the left regular module $\mathbb QS_n$. Over $\mathbb C$ the regular module is the direct sum of the complex Specht modules with multiplicities, and by [F2] the eigenvalues of $L_r$ on that module are the integers $c_T(r)$, the contents of the node containing $r$, over all standard tableaux $T$ of $n$ nodes; hence $h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-a)$ is squarefree with the integer roots in the finite set $E_r$. The group-basis coordinates of $h_r(L_r)$ are integers and vanish over $\mathbb Q$, so this identity holds already in $\mathbb ZS_n$. Reduction of coefficients modulo $p$ therefore gives $h_r(L_r)=0$ in $kS_n$, so the minimal polynomial $f_r$ of $L_r$ on the regular module $kS_n$ divides the reduction $\bar h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-\bar a)$ in $k[X]$, and every root of $f_r$ lies in the image $\mathbb F_p$ of $\mathbb Z$ in $k$.

*Antipode invariance.* The antipode $\sigma:kS_n\to kS_n$, $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$, is an anti-automorphism fixing every transposition, hence fixes each $L_r$ and therefore each $P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]$ and each $e(\mathbf i)$.

*An integral central identity.* In $\mathbb ZS_n$ one has $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{c(g)}g$, where $c(g)$ is the number of cycles, including fixed points. To prove this by induction, regard $S_{n-1}$ as fixing $n$. A term multiplied by $u$ leaves $n$ fixed and adds one cycle. A term multiplied by $(a,n)$ inserts $n$ in the cycle containing $a$, without changing its cycle count. Conversely, deleting a nonfixed $n$ from its cycle uniquely recovers the permutation in $S_{n-1}$ and the transposition used. Thus every permutation occurs exactly once. Comparing coefficients, each elementary symmetric polynomial $C_s$ in $L_1,\ldots,L_n$ is a sum of all permutations with $n-s$ cycles and hence is central; the identity and centrality remain true after reduction to $k$.

*Primary projectors.* Write $f_r=\prod_{a\in\mathbb F_p}(X-a)^{m_a}$ with $m_a\ge0$. For $a\ne b$ the ideals $\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ and $\big((X-b)^{m_b}\big)$ of $k[X]$ are comaximal, since two powers of distinct linear polynomials are coprime and Bezout gives $1=u(X)(X-a)^{m_a}+v(X)(X-b)^{m_b}$. By [F4] applied to the ring $k[X]/(f_r)$ and its comaximal ideals, the canonical map $k[X]/(f_r)\to\prod_{a:m_a>0}k[X]/\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ is an isomorphism; let $\varepsilon_{r,a}$ be the preimage of the idempotent supported at the $a$-th factor when $m_a>0$, and put $\varepsilon_{r,a}=0$ when $m_a=0$. Then $\sum_a\varepsilon_{r,a}=1$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}^2=\varepsilon_{r,a}$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}\varepsilon_{r,b}=0$ for $a\ne b$, and $(X-a)^{m_a}\varepsilon_{r,a}=0$ in $k[X]/(f_r)$. Substituting the algebra element $L_r$ for $X$ (legitimate because $f_r(L_r)=0$) gives elements $P_{r,a}:=\varepsilon_{r,a}(L_r)\in k[L_r]$ with $\sum_aP_{r,a}=1$, $P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a}$ and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}P_{r,a}=0$.

*These are the primary projections.* Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module. Since the $P_{r,a}$ are polynomials in $L_r$, they commute with $L_r$ and with one another; as $1=\sum_aP_{r,a}$ one has $M=\sum_aP_{r,a}M$, and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}$ annihilates $P_{r,a}M$, so $P_{r,a}M\subseteq M_{r,a}$. Conversely, if $m\in M_{r,a}$, then $(L_r-a)^Nm=0$ for $N\ge m_a$, and for $b\ne a$ the element $L_r-b=(a-b)+(L_r-a)$ is invertible on the $a$-primary subspace because $(a-b)\in k^\times$ and $(L_r-a)$ is nilpotent there; from $P_{r,b}(L_r-b)^{m_b}=0$ we get $P_{r,b}m=0$ for $b\ne a$, whence $m=P_{r,a}m$. Thus $P_{r,a}M=M_{r,a}$ and $M=\bigoplus_aM_{r,a}$. The products $e(\mathbf i)=\prod_rP_{r,i_r}$ are idempotent, pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$ by multiplicativity of the $P_{r,a}$; applying the same argument successively to the commuting operators $L_1,\dots,L_n$ gives $e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$.

*Central CRT separates contents.* Choose $N\ge1$ such that $(L_r-i_r)^Ne(\mathbf i)=0$ for every $r$ and every tuple $\mathbf i$, using step 2.1 and the finiteness of the indices. On the commutative algebra summand $e(\mathbf i)k[L_1,\ldots,L_n]$ with identity $e(\mathbf i)$, the commuting elements $(L_r-i_r)e(\mathbf i)$ generate an ideal whose $D$-th power is zero for $D=n(N-1)+1$: every monomial of degree $D$ has a factor with exponent at least $N$. Thus $C_s-c_s(\mathbf i)$ belongs to that nilpotent ideal, where $c_s(\mathbf i)$ is the elementary symmetric function of the residues. The tuple $c(\mathbf i)=(c_1(\mathbf i),\ldots,c_n(\mathbf i))$ determines the content, because $\prod_r(X-i_r)=\sum_{s=0}^n(-1)^sc_s(\mathbf i)X^{n-s}$ determines the multiplicities of its distinct linear factors, over every characteristic. In $R=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]$, the distinct content tuples therefore define distinct pairwise comaximal maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_\alpha=(Y_s-c_s(\alpha):1\le s\le n)$; their powers $\mathfrak m_\alpha^D$ are also pairwise comaximal, since expanding $1=(a+b)^{2D-1}$ for $a+b=1$ places every term in one of the two $D$-th powers. By [F4], choose $Q_\alpha\in R$ congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak m_\alpha^D$ and to $0$ modulo every other $\mathfrak m_\beta^D$. The nilpotence just proved gives $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)e(\mathbf i)=e(\mathbf i)$ when $\mathbf i\in I_\alpha$, and $0$ otherwise. Since the tuple idempotents sum to $1$, it follows that $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)=e_\alpha$. This is central by step 1.3. Idempotency, pairwise orthogonality for distinct content classes, and $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_n}e_\alpha=1$ follow from step 3.1 and the partition of all tuples into their content classes.

*The functor projectors.* Fix $i\in\mathbb F_p$ and $\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$. The primary projectors for $L_r$, $r<n$, computed in $kS_{n-1}$ agree with those in $kS_n$: the primary idempotents in $k[L_r]$ are uniquely determined by their congruences modulo the powers of the distinct linear factors of the minimal polynomial, and the inclusion preserves the polynomial relations of $L_r$. Summing once over each distinct sequence representing $\alpha$ gives $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i))=e_\alpha^{(n-1)}P_{n,i}$. By step 4.1 the first factor is central in $kS_{n-1}$, while the second commutes with $kS_{n-1}$ by [F1]; their product is therefore an idempotent commuting with that subgroup algebra. The sets $\{(\mathbf j,i):\mathbf j\in I_\alpha\}$ are disjoint for distinct pairs $(\alpha,i)$ and partition all tuples of length $n$. Consequently these idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, and their images are $kS_{n-1}$-submodules. Grouping these actual direct summands by the last residue gives $\operatorname{Res}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb F_p}E_iM$. The indexing is by content classes throughout, so no content is counted twice.

*Every nonzero content summand has local center.* Fix $e=e_\alpha\ne0$. Since $e$ is central, $Z(e kS_n)=eZ(kS_n)$: an element central in the summand commutes with the complementary summand because their products vanish. By [F7] every element of this center is $ef(L)$ for a symmetric polynomial $f$ over $k$. For every $\mathbf i\in I_\alpha$, the difference $(f(L)-f(\mathbf i))e(\mathbf i)$ belongs to the nilpotent ideal of step 4.1; symmetry makes $f(\mathbf i)$ the same scalar $a=f(\alpha)$ for all these tuples. The orthogonal sum of these differences is nilpotent with the common exponent $D$ of that step. Hence every central element of the summand has the form $ae+u$ with $u$ nilpotent. The scalar $a$ is unique: a nonzero scalar multiple of $e$ is invertible in this nonzero summand and cannot be nilpotent. As the center is commutative, sums of commuting nilpotents and their products with any central element are nilpotent. Thus its nilpotents form an ideal, the scalar map is a surjective ring homomorphism onto $k$, and every element with nonzero scalar is invertible by the finite geometric series. The center is local over the original field $k$, without extending scalars.

*Induction side.* The same computation with $n$ replaced by $d+1$ shows that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_{d+1}$ commuting with $kS_d$, that $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$ with pairwise orthogonal summands, and that $kS_{d+1}=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$; hence for any finite-dimensional $M$, $$kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M=\bigoplus_iF_iM,$$ the middle step using $M=\bigoplus_\alpha e_\alpha M$ and the centrality of $e_\alpha$ in $kS_d$. This is $\operatorname{Ind}M=\bigoplus_iF_iM$.

*Primitivity and exhaustiveness.* A central idempotent $b$ in $e kS_n$ has scalar $0$ or $1$ by step 5.2. In the first case $b$ is nilpotent and idempotent, so $b=0$; in the second case $e-b$ is nilpotent and idempotent, so $b=e$. Thus each nonzero $e_\alpha$ is primitive central. Their orthogonal sum is $1$ by step 4.1. Any primitive central idempotent $b$ of $kS_n$ decomposes as $\sum_\alpha be_\alpha$ into orthogonal central idempotents; primitivity leaves exactly one nonzero term, and the primitivity of that $e_\alpha$ forces $b=e_\alpha$. By [F6] these are precisely the block idempotents. At rank zero $kS_0=k$ and $e(\varnothing)=1$ gives the unique block; restriction from rank zero is taken to be the zero functor, while induction to rank one has only residue $0$. This convention does not invoke a group $S_{-1}$.

*Exactness and duality.* Each $E_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$; a map $f:M\to N$ of $kS_n$-modules commutes with the action of the element $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, so it restricts to a map $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M\to e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}N$, and each such functor is exact as a direct summand of the identity, hence additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. Each $F_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$, which are direct summands of induction $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M$; by [F5] $kS_{d+1}$ is free as a right $kS_d$-module, so induction, and with it each $F_i$, is exact, additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. For duality observe that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is fixed by the antipode by step 1.2, and that the standard nondegenerate pairing $M\times M^*\to k$ satisfies $(xm,f)=(m,x^*f)$; hence for finite-dimensional $M$ the transpose of the projection on $M$ is the projection on $M^*$ and $(e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M)^*\cong e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M^*$, giving $E_i(M)^*\cong E_i(M^*)$. All these restriction-duality identifications are $k$-linear and natural.

*Induction duality by a perfect coset pairing.* Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $\pi_H:kG\to kH$ retain the coefficients of the elements of $H$. For a finite-dimensional left $kH$-module $M$, with contragredient action $(a f)(m)=f(a^{-1}m)$, define $\langle g\otimes m,h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}g)m)$ between $\operatorname{Ind}M$ and $\operatorname{Ind}M^*$. For $a\in H$, the $kH$-bimodule property of $\pi_H$ gives $\pi_H(h^{-1}ga)=\pi_H(h^{-1}g)a$ and $\pi_H((ha)^{-1}g)=a^{-1}\pi_H(h^{-1}g)$; these identities prove balancing in the first and second tensor factors, respectively. Simultaneous left multiplication of $g,h$ by any element of $G$ leaves $h^{-1}g$ unchanged, proving $G$-invariance. On a finite left-coset transversal $T$ one has $\pi_H(s^{-1}r)=\delta_{s,r}1$ for $r,s\in T$. Thus the pairing is the direct sum of the perfect evaluations $M\times M^*\to k$ and is perfect by [F5]. For $e=e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, right multiplication $R_e(g\otimes m)=ge\otimes m$ is a well-defined $G$-linear idempotent because $e$ commutes with $kH$. Let $\tau:kG\to k$ be the coefficient of $1$; directly on group elements, $\tau(xy)=\tau(yx)$. For every $b\in H$, the coefficient of $b$ in $ze$ equals $\tau(b^{-1}ze)=\tau(eb^{-1}z)=\tau(b^{-1}ez)$, since $e$ commutes with $b$. Therefore $\pi_H(ze)=\pi_H(ez)$ for all $z\in kG$. Writing $e^*$ for its antipode image, step 1.2 gives $e^*=e$, so expansion in the group basis yields $\langle R_e(g\otimes m),h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}ge)m)=f(\pi_H(eh^{-1}g)m)=\langle g\otimes m,R_e(h\otimes f)\rangle$. The two images of $R_e$ pair perfectly: a vector in either image annihilating the other annihilates the entire opposite space, since the opposite kernel is orthogonal to that image, and hence vanishes by perfectness. By tensor balancing, $ge\otimes m=ge\otimes e_\alpha m$, so these images are precisely $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M$ and $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M^*$. Distinct $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ images are orthogonal by self-adjointness and projector orthogonality. Summing the perfect image pairings over $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$ proves the natural $G$-isomorphism $F_i(M^*)\cong F_i(M)^*$; invariance supplies the contragredient action, and evaluation shows naturality in $M$. The construction uses finite transversals and holds over every characteristic, including $2$.

*Partition content agrees with the block content.* Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $\alpha$ be the multiset of its node contents reduced modulo $p$. Over $\mathbb C$, [F2] makes every elementary symmetric $C_s$ act on $S^\lambda$ by the integer $c_s(\lambda)$. In the integral basis of [F8] the matrix of $C_s-c_s(\lambda)$ has integer entries and vanishes after tensoring with $\mathbb C$, so it vanishes integrally and after specialization to $k$. Thus the CRT polynomial $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)$ of step 4.1 acts as $1$ on $S^\lambda_k$, while the other content projections act as zero. The same is true on its nonzero subquotients. Hence any simple module obtained from this Specht module belongs to the block $e_\alpha$, establishing the stated content dictionary without a splitting-field descent or a reduced interpolation denominator.

boundaries.evidence: A partition with no i-nodes has the empty word, which the definition already treats as reduced; the reduction and both selections are vacuous, so ε_i = φ_i = 0 and the definition assigns no good or cogood node.
Zeros are the cancelled positions of the word and the definition deletes them before the signs are read; residue 0 is an ordinary value of i, so a 0-node is treated like any other node.
A single i-node gives a one-letter reduced word (+ or −) and is selected as cogood or good accordingly; the definition also records that the survived signs have the shape + …… + − …… −.

The confluence argument recorded in the definition makes the reduced word and the outermost signs independent of the order of replacements, so the degenerate case of several possible cancellations has a unique outcome.
The good node is defined as the topmost surviving − and the cogood node as the bottommost surviving +; these endpoint selections and their uniqueness are part of the definition.
All lists are finite, ordered top to bottom, and the reduction is deterministic; no choice principle is used, as recorded in the definition statement.

Forward direction of the dictionary stated in the definition: a removable node that is normal in the c−r signature has a normal transpose in Brundan’s r−c convention, since the residue sign is reversed and transposed nodes reverse the order in their residue class, as recorded in the definition from Brundan’s transposed-node remark.

Reverse direction of the same dictionary: a removable node whose transpose is normal in Brundan’s convention is normal in the c−r signature, because transposition is an involution and the residue sign reversal is symmetric, so the two conventions match in both directions, as stated in the definition.

citations.quote: For $H\le G$, restriction forgets from $\mathbb Z[G]$ to $\mathbb Z[H]$. For a left $H$-module $M$, set $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=\mathbb Z[G]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[H]}M$ and $\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z[H]}(\mathbb Z[G],M)$, with $G$ acting on the latter by $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$.
For $H\le G$, induction is left adjoint and coinduction is right adjoint to restriction.
If $H\le G$ and a left (respectively right) coset transversal is supplied, then $\mathbb Z[G]$ is free as a right (respectively left) $\mathbb Z[H]$-module on it.

boundaries.reason: The lemma concerns a finite group G and a subgroup H; groups are nonempty, and the only empty object is the zero module, which is disposed of by the zero case.

boundaries.evidence: M = 0 makes Ind and Coind zero and Φ_0 = 0, an isomorphism; steps 1.1 and 1.2 apply to the zero map and the isomorphism claims are trivial.
H = G: the transversal T of step 1.2 is a singleton, the sums of steps 2.1 and 2.2 have one term, and Φ is the standard identification Ind ≅ M ≅ Coind.
No hypothesis on k is imposed, so the case of a field whose characteristic divides |G| is included; step 3.1 records that the proof only multiplies and sums group elements and never divides.
The extreme subgroups H = 1 and H = G are included: for H = 1 the transversal is G itself, finite by hypothesis, and steps 2.1 and 2.2 apply; H = G is the singleton case.
The only selection is the finite transversal T of step 1.2; step 3.1 records that T is chosen by least elements, so no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The lemma states an isomorphism and adjointness consequences, not a biconditional, so no forward implication slot applies.
No converse direction is asserted by this lemma.

derivations.claim: $\Phi_M$ is a well-defined $kG$-linear map. For fixed $g,m$ the formula defines a function on $G$: if $xg\in H$ then $(xg)m\in M$, otherwise $0$. It is $k$-linear in $x$ by definition, and it is $kH$-linear: for $h\in H$ and $x\in G$, $\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(hx)=((hx)g)m$ if $hxg\in H$ and $0$ otherwise; since $hxg=(hx)g$ and $hxg\in H\iff xg\in H$ (as $h,h^{-1}\in H$), this equals $h((xg)m)=h\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x)$ in the first case and $0$ in the second. Hence $\Phi_M(g\otimes m)\in\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM$. The map is $k$-linear and in the second tensor variable balanced: for $h\in H$, the functions $\Phi_M(gh\otimes m)$ and $\Phi_M(g\otimes hm)$ both send $x$ to $((xg)h)m=(xg)(hm)$ when $xg\in H$ and to $0$ otherwise; so $\Phi_M$ is well defined on the tensor product. Finally it is $kG$-linear: $\Phi_M(g_0g\otimes m)(x)=((xg_0)g)m$ if $xg_0g\in H$ and $0$ otherwise, and $(g_0\Phi_M(g\otimes m))(x)=\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(xg_0)=((xg_0)g)m$ if $xg_0g\in H$ and $0$ otherwise, the two conditions being the same.

The inverse on coinduced maps. For $\varphi\in\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM$, define $\Psi_M(\varphi)=\sum_{t\in T}t\otimes\varphi(t^{-1})$. This is a finite sum and a $k$-linear map. Inverting the left cosets $tH$ shows that the right cosets $Ht^{-1}$ partition $G$. If a representative is replaced by $t'=th$ with $h\in H$, then $t'\otimes\varphi(t'^{-1})=th\otimes\varphi(h^{-1}t^{-1})=th\otimes h^{-1}\varphi(t^{-1})=t\otimes\varphi(t^{-1})$, by $kH$-linearity and the balancing relation. Thus the inverse formula is independent of the finite transversal.

$\Phi_M\Psi_M=\mathrm{id}$. For $x\in G$, there is exactly one $t_0\in T$ for which $x\in Ht_0^{-1}$, equivalently $xt_0\in H$. Write $x=ht_0^{-1}$. Then $\Phi_M(\Psi_M(\varphi))(x)=\sum_{t\in T,\ xt\in H}(xt)\varphi(t^{-1})=h\varphi(t_0^{-1})=\varphi(x)$, using the right-coset partition from step 1.2 and $kH$-linearity. Equality on the group basis gives equality on $kG$.

$\Psi_M\Phi_M=\mathrm{id}$. For $g\in G$ and $m\in M$, write uniquely $g=t_0h$ with $t_0\in T$ and $h\in H$. Then $\Psi_M(\Phi_M(g\otimes m))=\sum_{t\in T,\ t^{-1}g\in H}t\otimes(t^{-1}g)m=t_0\otimes hm=g\otimes m$, by the left-coset partition and tensor balancing. Since such elementary tensors span the induced module, this proves the second inverse identity.

Naturality and consequences. If $f:M\to M'$ is a $kH$-map, then for all $g,m,x$ one has $\Phi_{M'}(g\otimes f(m))(x)=f(\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x))$, because the formula is evaluated by multiplication in $M$ or $M'$ and $f$ is linear; hence $\Phi$ is a natural transformation, and by steps 2.1 and 2.2 each $\Phi_M$ is an isomorphism with natural inverse $\Psi_M$. Therefore $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\cong\operatorname{Coind}_H^G$ as functors, and [F2] yields that induction is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction: the left adjunction is its induction adjunction, and the right adjunction is transported across this natural isomorphism from the coinduction adjunction. Induction $kG\otimes_{kH}-$ is right exact, and coinduction $\operatorname{Hom}_{kH}(kG,-)$ is left exact; a natural isomorphism between the two functors therefore makes induction exact, in agreement with the freeness of $kG$ over $kH$ recorded in [F3]. No hypothesis on $k$, on characteristic, or on splitting is used, and the only selection made is the finite transversal $T$ of least representatives.

Includes H=G, trivial groups, zero/infinite-dimensional M, characteristic 2 and nonsplitting k. Integral group-ring formulas extend coefficientwise to k; finite choice only.

citations.quote:
**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Steps 1.1–17.1 also prove the following restriction endpoint, independently
of the uncoloured-socle corollary: for every $p$-restricted $\xi\vdash m$
with $m\ge1$,
$$\operatorname{soc}E_iD(\xi)=\begin{cases}D(\xi\setminus A_i),&\varepsilon_i(\xi)>0,\\0,&\varepsilon_i(\xi)=0,\end{cases}$$
where $A_i$ is the good $i$-node and its deletion remains $p$-restricted.
The scalar is the node residue in step 16.1. The proof covers every field
of characteristic $p$, including $p=2$, using the unused coordinate
$N=m+1$ and the degree-zero lower corner when $m=1$.

Let $F$ be a field, $n\ge0$, $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\lambda'$ be the
conjugate partition. Write $\Omega_\lambda$ for the finite set of
$\lambda$-tabloids and let
$$M^\lambda_F=F^{(\Omega_\lambda)},\qquad S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad \kappa_t=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma,\qquad e_t=\kappa_t\{t\}$$
be the field-valued tabloid module, the span of the polytabloids inside it,
the column antisymmetrizer, and the polytabloid of a $\lambda$-tableau $t$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). Let
$$\beta_F:M^\lambda_F\times M^\lambda_F\longrightarrow F$$
be the $F$-bilinear form for which the tabloid basis is orthonormal
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]), and for a
subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_F$ put
$$V^\perp:=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}.$$

Let $\operatorname{sgn}$ be the sign representation of $S_n$ on the line
$F w$, so that $\sigma\cdot w=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)w$
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]]), and let
$$S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$$
be the tensor product of $F[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w):=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, a
finite-dimensional $F[S_n]$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]). For a
finite-dimensional $F[S_n]$-module $D$ the **dual** is
$D^*=\operatorname{Hom}_F(D,F)$ with $(\sigma\cdot f)(v):=f(\sigma^{-1}v)$.

Fix the **row-filled** $\lambda$-tableau $t_0$, whose $i$-th row carries the
block $B_i=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$
in increasing order, and let $t_0^{\mathsf T}$ be its transpose, a
$\lambda'$-tableau. For a $\lambda'$-tableau $u$ let $\sigma_u\in S_n$ be the
unique permutation with $\sigma_u\cdot t_0^{\mathsf T}=u$, and let
$u^{\mathsf T}$ be the transpose of $u$, a $\lambda$-tableau. Define an
$F$-linear map on the tabloid basis of $M^{\lambda'}_F$ by
$$\theta(\{u\}):=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma_u)\,\bigl(e_{u^{\mathsf T}}\otimes w\bigr) \ \in\ S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$

**Lemma.** With this notation:

1. $\theta$ does not depend on the chosen representative $u$ of the tabloid
   $\{u\}$; it is a well-defined $F[S_n]$-module homomorphism
   $\theta:M^{\lambda'}_F\to S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ with
   $\theta(\{t_0^{\mathsf T}\})=e_{t_0}\otimes w$.
2. $\theta$ is surjective and
   $\ker\theta=(S^{\lambda'}_F)^\perp$.
3. Consequently $\theta$ induces $F[S_n]$-isomorphisms
   $$M^{\lambda'}_F/(S^{\lambda'}_F)^\perp\cong S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong (S^{\lambda'}_F)^*,$$
   the second being the composite with $x\mapsto\beta_F(x,\cdot)|_{S^{\lambda'}_F}$.

No nondegeneracy of $\beta_F$ restricted to $S^{\lambda'}_F$ is assumed, and
the statement includes every prime characteristic, the case $n=0$, and the
case $F=\mathbb Q$ used in step 2.2. No step divides by a group order, none
uses positivity or averaging, and none uses characteristic zero beyond the
explicitly separated rational computation in steps 2.2 and 3.1.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p$, let $n\ge0$,
and let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with $\lambda$ $p$-regular. Let
$$M^\mu_F=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\mu_{\mathbb Z},\qquad S^\mu_F\subseteq M^\mu_F,\qquad R^\mu_F=S^\mu_F\cap(S^\mu_F)^{\perp},\qquad D^\mu_F=S^\mu_F/R^\mu_F$$
be the field-valued tabloid module with its orthonormal form $\beta_F$, the
field-valued Specht span, the form radical of its restriction and the
quotient ([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]],
[[thm-specht-radical-quotient-is-nonzero-exactly-for-p-regular-partitions]]),
and let $U\le M^\mu_F$ be an $F[S_n]$-submodule. Then:

1. **Dominance.** Every nonzero $F[S_n]$-homomorphism
   $\varphi:S^\lambda_F\to M^\mu_F/U$ satisfies $\lambda\unrhd\mu$.
2. **Equality case.** If $\lambda=\mu$, then the image of such a nonzero
   $\varphi$ is exactly the image $(S^\mu_F+U)/U$ of $S^\mu_F$ in
   $M^\mu_F/U$; in particular $U$ does not contain $S^\mu_F$.
3. **Quotient form.** Statements 1 and 2 remain true with $S^\lambda_F$
   replaced by $D^\lambda_F$: every nonzero $F[S_n]$-homomorphism
   $\psi:D^\lambda_F\to M^\mu_F/U$ satisfies $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, and if
   $\lambda=\mu$ then its image is $(S^\mu_F+U)/U$ and
   $U\nsupseteq S^\mu_F$.
4. **Separation.** If $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are both $p$-regular and
   $D^\lambda_F\cong D^\mu_F$ as $F[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$. More
   generally, if $\lambda$ is $p$-regular and $D^\lambda_F\cong D^\mu_F$,
   then $\mu$ is $p$-regular and $\mu=\lambda$.

No simplicity of $S^\lambda_F$ or $S^\mu_F$ is assumed or claimed, the case
$U=0$ (no submodule divided out) is included, and $n=0$ and characteristic
$2$ need no separate treatment. No step averages over a group, divides by a
group order, or uses positivity of any form.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $F$ be a
field of characteristic $p$. Let $\beta_F$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form on $M^\lambda_F=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, with
orthonormal tabloid basis, and let
$$S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad R^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F\cap(S^\lambda_F)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F/R^\lambda_F,$$
where $V^{\perp}=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]],
[[thm-james-submodule-theorem-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Let $G_\lambda$ be
the Gram matrix of the integral tabloid form in the standard-polytabloid
basis of the integral Specht lattice $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, and let
$g_\lambda$ be the positive greatest common divisor of its entries
([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]],
[[lem-specht-gram-gcd-detects-p-regularity]]). Write $G_\lambda\bmod p$ for
the entrywise image of $G_\lambda$ in $F$, a matrix with entries in $F$.
Then:

1. **Vanishing criterion.**
   $$D^\lambda_F=0\iff p\mid G_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j \iff p\mid g_\lambda\iff\lambda\text{ is not }p\text{-regular},$$
   and equivalently $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ if and only if $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for
   every $j\ge1$, where $z_j(\lambda)$ is the number of parts of $\lambda$
   equal to $j$.
2. **Dimension.** $\dim_FD^\lambda_F=\operatorname{rank}_F(G_\lambda\bmod p)$;
   this dimension is determined by $\lambda$ and $p$ alone, and it is
   positive exactly when $\lambda$ is $p$-regular.
3. **Structure when nonzero.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then
   $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ is the simple, self-dual and absolutely irreducible
   head of $S^\lambda_F$, and $R^\lambda_F$ is the unique maximal submodule
   of $S^\lambda_F$, equal to the module radical
   $\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_F)$.

For the $k$ of a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$,
$D^\lambda_k$ is the modular Specht quotient $D^\lambda$ of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], so the criterion above
decides for which $\lambda$ that quotient vanishes. No simplicity of
$S^\lambda_F$ itself is asserted.

The case ε_i(μ) = 0 is where the summand vanishes: step 1.2 sets soc(E_iD(μ)) = 0 then and the displayed sum omits that residue.
d = 1 is worked in step 4.1: the display has the single term D(∅) and soc(D(μ)↓_{S_0}) = k = D(∅).
p = 2 is allowed: step 1.1 decomposes over i ∈ Z/2 and step 1.2 invokes the local restriction endpoint proof, applied in every positive characteristic in the statement.
No residue class is special: steps 1.2 and 2.1 sum over all i ∈ Z/p and step 3.1 compares any pair i ≠ j.
The residues and good nodes are finite in number and canonically determined by the definition; no choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the restriction decomposes as $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iD(\mu)$ with each $E_iD(\mu)$ a $kS_{d-1}$-submodule, and by [F5] the socle of the restriction is the direct sum $\bigoplus_i\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))$.

By the local restriction argument [F3], for each residue $i$ the module $\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))$ is $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$ and is $0$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; by [F3] each $\mu\setminus A_i$ is a $p$-restricted partition of $d-1$, so each displayed $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ is a simple $kS_{d-1}$-module by [F4].

Summing the descriptions of step 1.2 over the finitely many residues $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and using step 1.1 gives $$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i).$$

The sum is multiplicity-free and its summands are pairwise non-isomorphic: if $i\ne j$ and both $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varepsilon_j(\mu)$ are positive, then the good nodes $A_i$ and $A_j$ have different residues and are therefore distinct nodes of $\mu$, so the $p$-restricted partitions $\mu\setminus A_i$ and $\mu\setminus A_j$ of $d-1$ are distinct by [F2]; by [F4] their simple modules $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ and $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ are non-isomorphic. Each residue contributes its summand once, so each isomorphism class occurs with multiplicity one in the displayed socle.

The displayed decomposition of step 2.1 has the left-hand side $\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}(D(\mu)\downarrow_{S_{d-1}})$ and, by step 3.1, is a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules with one summand per residue $i$ satisfying $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$. No claim is made here about the restriction being semisimple. In the smallest case $d=1$ one has $\mu=(1)$, and the only node of residue $0$ is the removable node $(1,1)$, so $\varepsilon_0(\mu)=1$ and the right-hand side is the single term $D(\varnothing)=k$, while the restriction to the trivial group $S_0$ is $k$ itself, in agreement with the display; this is the smallest instance in which the summands carry the empty partition as a label.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition of $n\ge0$ with
parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge1$ and conjugate partition
$\lambda'$, whose $j$-th part is the number $\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\ge j\}$
of nodes of $[\lambda]$ in column $j$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $j\ge1$ let
$$z_j(\lambda):=\#\{\,i:\lambda_i=j\,\}$$
be the multiplicity with which the positive integer $j$ occurs as a part of
$\lambda$; only finitely many $z_j$ are nonzero.

- $\lambda$ is **$p$-regular** when every positive part of $\lambda$ occurs
  fewer than $p$ times, that is, when $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for every $j\ge1$.
- $\lambda$ is **$p$-restricted** when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<p$ for every
  $i\ge1$, where the sequence is padded by the trailing zeros
  $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>k$.

Both conditions are finite families of inequalities. For $i>k$ one has
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}=0<p$, so the restrictedness condition is the finite
list for $1\le i\le k$. The empty partition $\varnothing\vdash0$ has no parts
and $k=0$, so $z_j(\varnothing)=0<p$ and $0-0=0<p$ for every $j,i\ge1$: it is
simultaneously $p$-regular and $p$-restricted for every prime $p$.

The two conditions are exchanged by conjugation: **$\lambda$ is $p$-restricted
if and only if $\lambda'$ is $p$-regular.** The number of columns of $[\lambda]$
of height exactly $i$ is the difference $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ of consecutive
parts, and these heights are precisely the parts of $\lambda'$, so the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$; the
stated equivalence compares the same integers with $p$.

The names record two genuinely different label conventions used later on this
page: James's modular simple modules $D^\lambda$ are labelled by **$p$-regular**
$\lambda$. Dual Specht modules themselves are defined for every partition;
their simple heads give the **$p$-restricted** labelling of simple modules,
related to the first convention by transposition and a sign twist. Neither
class of partitions contains the other in general.

boundaries.evidence: For the empty partition the only 0-node is the addable node (1,1), so f̃_0∅ = (1) while ẽ_i∅ is undefined for every i; this is the base case used in steps 5.1 and 6.1.
Residue 0 is ordinary: the empty partition has a cogood addition in residue 0 and the operators are defined for i = 0 like any other residue (step 6.1).
Rank 1 is covered by steps 3.1 and 4.1: deleting the single removable node and adding the single cogood node are inverse moves, and step 5.1 states the inverse property for all ranks.
p = 2 is included: step 3.2 uses only the inequality μ_{r−1} − μ_r ≤ p − 1 and step 3.3 the analogous one, so both restrictedness proofs apply verbatim at p = 2, where differences are at most 1.
The endpoint selections are exactly step 2.1: the first surviving − and the last surviving + are compared there, and steps 3.1 and 4.1 transfer the comparison to partitions.
The operators are defined by deterministic finite selections from the reduced word; no choice principle is used, as recorded in step 6.1.
Forward: if ν = ẽ_iμ then the good node A of μ is cogood in ν and f̃_iν = ν ∪ A = μ, proved in step 5.1 from step 3.1.
Reverse: if μ = f̃_iν then the cogood node B of ν is good in μ and ẽ_iμ = μ ∖ B = ν, proved in step 5.1 from step 4.1.

derivations.claim: *The stack algorithm computes the normal form.* The stack algorithm of [F3] terminates with a word containing no $-$ before a $+$ (a surviving $-$ stays on the stack and blocks the stack from being empty, so no later $+$ survives after it), and the reduction relation is confluent by [F3], so the surviving signs read in order are the reduced signature with zero entries deleted, $+^a-^b$; in particular the good node corresponds to the first surviving $-$ and the cogood node to the last surviving $+$.

*Comparison of the $i$-words.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and $X$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$; put $
u:=\mu\setminus X$. By [F2] the $i$-nodes of $
u$ are obtained from those of $\mu$ by removing $X$ from the removable list and inserting $X$ into the addable list, all other $i$-nodes and their top-to-bottom order being unchanged; hence the $i$-signature words of $\mu$ and $
u$ have the same length and the same entries except at the position $p$ of $X$, where the word of $\mu$ has $-$ and the word of $
u$ has $+$.
derivations.justification: Only rows r-1,r,r+1 can change boundary status. Every changed boundary other than X has residue i+1 or i-1; p is prime and at least 2, so neither equals i. A row-(r+1) addable may disappear, but only at residue i-1.

derivations.claim: *First surviving $-$ versus last surviving $+$.* Let $w$ be a signature word with $w_p=-$, let $w'$ be $w$ with the entry at $p$ changed to $+$, let $u$ be the prefix of $w$ strictly before $p$, and let $s$ be the suffix strictly after $p$. We prove that $p$ is the position of the first surviving $-$ of $w$ if and only if $p$ is the position of the last surviving $+$ of $w'$. Let $S$ be the stack of [F3] after scanning $u$; the prefix of $w'$ before $p$ is the same word $u$, so the same stack $S$ is present there. If $S$ is nonempty, let $q$ be its bottom entry; scanning $w$ further, $q$ can leave the stack only by being cancelled by a $+$ that has first cancelled every entry above it, in particular the entry at $p$, so either $q$ survives, giving a surviving $-$ before $p$, or the entry $p$ is cancelled before $q$ and does not survive; in both cases $p$ is not the first surviving $-$ of $w$. Similarly, scanning $w'$ the entry at $p$ is a $+$, which survives only if the stack just before it is empty, so if $S$ is nonempty then $p$ does not survive and is not the last surviving $+$ of $w'$. Hence both events force $S$ to be empty, and we may assume this. With $S$ empty, push the $-$ at $p$ in the scan of $w$; while this entry is alive, the pending entries above it after scanning a prefix $q$ of $s$ are the $-$ signs of $q$ not yet cancelled, and since no $+$ has yet occurred at height $0$, that number is $\#-(q)-\#+(q)$. Consequently $p$ is cancelled at the first $+$ of $s$ whose preceding prefix $q$ has $\#+(q)=\#-(q)$, and such a $+$ exists if and only if some prefix $q$ of $s$ has $\#+(q)>\#-(q)$: counts change by one at each symbol, so a strict surplus arises only across a step of equality, and conversely a prefix with equality followed by a $+$ would create a strict surplus. Thus, with $S$ empty, the entry at $p$ survives in $w$ if and only if $$(C)\quad \#+(q)\le\#-(q)\quad\text{for every prefix }q\text{ of }s.$$ In $w'$, the $+$ at $p$ arrives at the empty stack $S$ and survives; after it, a later $+$ of $s$ survives exactly when the stack is empty at its arrival. If (C) holds and a $+$ of $s$ survived, with preceding prefix $q$, then all $-$ of $q$ were cancelled, so $\#-(q)\le\#+(q)$, while (C) applied to the prefix $q$ extended by that $+$ gives $\#+(q)+1\le\#-(q)$, a contradiction; hence no later $+$ survives. Conversely, if (C) fails then some $+$ of $s$ survives: the stack height after a prefix $q$ of $s$ equals $\#-(q)-\#+(q)+c(q)$, where $c(q)$ is the number of $+$ signs of $q$ that survived, as one checks by induction on the length of $q$ (a $-$ raises the height, and a $+$ raises $c$ by one and lowers the height by one exactly when it cancels); if no $+$ of $s$ survived then $c(q)=0$ for every prefix $q$, so $\#+(q)\le\#-(q)$ for every prefix, contradicting the failure of (C). Therefore (C) holds if and only if, in $w'$, the entry at $p$ is the last surviving $+$, and the claim follows.

*Good versus cogood for a removable node.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted, $X$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ and $
u=\mu\setminus X$. By step 1.2 the words of $\mu$ and $
u$ differ exactly by the flip at the position of $X$, so step 2.1 gives: $X$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$ if and only if $X$ is the cogood $i$-node of $
u$. Consequently, if $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$ and $X$ is the good $i$-node, then $\varphi_i(
u)>0$ with cogood node $X$, and $	ilde f_i(
u)=
u\cup X=\mu$.

*Removing the good node preserves restrictedness.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and let $A=(r,\mu_r)$ be its good $i$-node; we show that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$ is $p$-restricted. If $r\ge2$ and $\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r=p-1$, then $B:=(r-1,\mu_{r-1})$ is a removable node of $\mu$ (as $\mu_{r-1}>\mu_r$) with $\operatorname{res}(B)=\mu_{r-1}-(r-1)=\mu_r-r+p\equiv\mu_r-r=\operatorname{res}(A)$, so $B$ is a removable $i$-node above $A$ and hence occurs before $A$ in the $i$-word. There is no $i$-node between $B$ and $A$: these are consecutive rows, and any addable node in either row has residue $i+1$. Thus $B$ is still on the stack when $A$ is pushed. Either some $-$ before $A$ survives, and then $A$ is not the first surviving $-$, or every $-$ before $A$ is eventually cancelled, in particular $B$; but a $+$ cancels $B$ only after cancelling every entry pushed after $B$, in particular the entry at $A$, so in that case $A$ is cancelled and does not survive; both alternatives contradict that $A$ is good. Hence $\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r\le p-2$, and then $\nu$ is $p$-restricted: deleting the last node of row $r$ leaves $(\mu_r-1)-\mu_{r+1}\le p-2<p$ and, if $r\ge2$, $\mu_{r-1}-(\mu_r-1)=(\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r)+1\le p-1<p$, while all other consecutive differences are unchanged.
derivations.justification: When the preceding row difference is p-1, its removable B has the residue of A. They are in consecutive rows and any addable in either row has residue i+1, so B cannot be cancelled before A is pushed.

derivations.claim: *Adding the cogood node preserves restrictedness.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and let $B=(r,\mu_r+1)$ be its cogood $i$-node; we show that $\nu=\mu\cup B$ is $p$-restricted. Suppose first that $\mu_r-\mu_{r+1}=p-1$; then $D:=(r+1,\mu_{r+1}+1)$ is an addable $i$-node of $\mu$, because $\mu_r>\mu_{r+1}$ and $\operatorname{res}(D)=\mu_{r+1}-r\equiv\mu_r+1-r=\operatorname{res}(B)$; between $B$ and $D$ in the top-to-bottom order there is no $i$-node: the entries after $B$ in row $r$ do not exist, and the remaining $i$-node of row $r$ is the removable node $(r,\mu_r)$, whose residue is $\operatorname{res}(B)-1$, while the addable node of row $r+1$ is $D$ itself. Hence $B$ and $D$ are consecutive in the $i$-word, both with sign $+$. If the $+$ at $B$ survives, it leaves the stack empty, so the next entry, the $+$ at $D$, also survives and is later than $B$; if the $+$ at $B$ does not survive, then $B$ is not the cogood node. In both cases $B$ is not the last surviving $+$, contradicting that $B$ is cogood. Hence $\mu_r-\mu_{r+1}\le p-2$, and then $(\mu_r+1)-\mu_{r+1}\le p-1<p$, while $\mu_{r-1}-(\mu_r+1)=(\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r)-1<p$ for $r\ge2$ (no row above change is needed when $r=1$), and all other differences are unchanged; so $\nu$ is $p$-restricted.

*Good versus cogood for an addable node.* Let $Y$ be an addable $i$-node of $\mu$ and $
u:=\mu\cup Y$. The node $Y$ is removable in $
u$, and $\mu=
u\setminus Y$; applying step 3.1 to the pair $(
u,Y)$ gives: $Y$ is the good $i$-node of $
u$ if and only if $Y$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$. Consequently, if $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$ and $Y$ is the cogood $i$-node, then $\varepsilon_i(
u)>0$ with good node $Y$, and $	ilde e_i(
u)=
u\setminus Y=\mu$.

*The inverse property.* Let $\mu,
u$ be $p$-restricted partitions. If $
u=	ilde e_i\mu$, then $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, $
u=\mu\setminus A$ for the good $i$-node $A$ of $\mu$, and step 3.1 gives that $A$ is the cogood $i$-node of $
u$, so that $	ilde f_i
u=
u\cup A=\mu$. Conversely, if $\mu=	ilde f_i
u$, then $\varphi_i(
u)>0$, $\mu=
u\cup B$ for the cogood $i$-node $B$ of $
u$, and step 4.1 gives that $B$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$, so that $	ilde e_i\mu=\mu\setminus B=
u$. Hence $\mu=	ilde f_i
u\iff
u=	ilde e_i\mu$ for all $p$-restricted $\mu,
u$, both sides being false when the relevant node does not exist; and by steps 3.2 and 3.3 the operators map $p$-restricted partitions to $p$-restricted partitions.

*Conclusion.* By [F1] at most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node exist in each residue, so the partial operators are well defined; removing a node lowers the rank by one and adding a node raises it by one, so $\tilde e_i$ lowers and $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one; and by step 5.1 each operator is defined at exactly the images of the other, so they are mutual inverses on their domains. No module theory and no choice principle are used.

citations.quote: For $H\le G$, restriction forgets from $\mathbb Z[G]$ to $\mathbb Z[H]$. For a left $H$-module $M$, set $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=\mathbb Z[G]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[H]}M$ and $\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z[H]}(\mathbb Z[G],M)$, with $G$ acting on the latter by $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$.
If $H\le G$ and a left (respectively right) coset transversal is supplied, then $\mathbb Z[G]$ is free as a right (respectively left) $\mathbb Z[H]$-module on it.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted
partition of $d\ge1$; write $D(\mu)$ for the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
Let $A_i$ denote the good $i$-node of $\mu$, for those
$i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i),$$
a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules: distinct residues give
distinct summands. The sum runs over the residues $i$ with
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, one good node per such residue; the completely
reducible special case (the restriction is semisimple if and only if every
normal node is good, Kleshchev II Theorem 0.6) is a separate statement and is
not asserted here.

On the set of $p$-restricted partitions
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]) define partial operators
$\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]), the
operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most
one cogood node exist in each residue. No module-theoretic statement is made
here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.

derivations.claim: Restriction is faithful on nonzero modules. Let $M\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module and consider the multiplication map $\varphi:kS_d\otimes_{kS_{d-1}}M\to M$, $\varphi(g\otimes m)=gm$, where $M$ is regarded as a $kS_{d-1}$-module by restriction. It is $kS_d$-linear and surjective, since the image of $1\otimes m$ is $m$ and the elements $m$ span $M$; hence if the restriction of $M$ to $kS_{d-1}$ were zero, the tensor product would be zero and $M=0$, a contradiction. Therefore restriction sends no nonzero module to zero.

Nonzero finite-dimensional modules have nonzero socle: choosing a nonzero submodule of least positive dimension gives a simple submodule, so the socle, which is the sum of all simple submodules, is nonzero.
$D(\mu)$ is a nonzero simple $kS_d$-module by [F3], because $\mu$ is $p$-restricted.
Applying step 1.1 to $M=D(\mu)$ with $d\ge1$: since $D(\mu)\ne0$ by step 1.3, its restriction to $S_{d-1}$ is nonzero.
By step 1.2 applied to the nonzero finite-dimensional $kS_{d-1}$-module $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)$ from step 2.1, the socle $\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}(D(\mu)\downarrow_{S_{d-1}})$ is nonzero.

By the residue-refined socle theorem [F4], the socle is the multiplicity-free sum of the simple modules $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ over the residues $i$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$. Since this socle is nonzero by step 3.1, at least one residue satisfies $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$.

Fix such a residue $i$. By [F5] the good $i$-node $A_i$ exists, $
u:=\mu\setminus A_i$ is a $p$-restricted partition of $d-1$, and $\mu=	ilde f_i
u$ with $	ilde f_i
u=
u\cup A_i$.

Induction on $d$. We prove that every $p$-restricted partition of $d$ is reachable from $\varnothing$ by $d$ cogood additions. For $d=0$ the empty partition is the only partition and it is reached by the empty sequence. For $d\ge1$ and a $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ of $d$, if $\mu=\varnothing$ there is nothing to prove, and otherwise step 5.1 supplies a residue $i$ and a $p$-restricted partition $
u$ of $d-1$ with $\mu=	ilde f_i
u$; by the inductive hypothesis $
u=	ilde f_{i_{d-1}}\cdots	ilde f_{i_1}\varnothing$ for suitable residues, whence $\mu=	ilde f_i	ilde f_{i_{d-1}}\cdots	ilde f_{i_1}\varnothing$. The residue $i$ is selected as, say, the least residue with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, so no choice principle is used.

Good deletions carry every $p$-restricted partition to $\varnothing$. At each nonempty stage step 5.1 produces a good node and, by [F5], the partition obtained by deleting it is again $p$-restricted of rank one less; iterating $d$ times reaches the only partition of rank $0$, which is $\varnothing$; equivalently, by the inverse property in [F5], the two procedures are mutually inverse step by step.

Consequences for the graph. By definition the edges of the graph are the partial operations $\nu\mapsto\tilde f_i\nu$, so step 6.1 says exactly that every $p$-restricted partition is reached from $\varnothing$; step 7.1 says every vertex reaches $\varnothing$ by good deletions $\tilde e_i$. The empty partition is the unique partition of $0$, so it is the unique rank-$0$ vertex, and it has no incoming edge from a $p$-restricted partition because no partition of $-1$ exists; all ranks are finite. No step used the characteristic of $k$ beyond the existence of the socle theorem [F4], and no choice principle was used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of weak compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$; zero parts are allowed and give empty rows). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

For a weak composition $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$, define $T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ to be the fillings of $[\lambda]$ by $1,\ldots,d$ with exactly $\mu_i$ entries equal to $i$, weakly increasing rows and strictly increasing columns. Put $T_0(\lambda)= igcup_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ and $K_{\lambda\mu}:=|T_0(\lambda,\mu)|$. This explicitly extends the partition-content definition of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] to weak compositions, including internal zero counts; a zero count means that its label is absent. The set is finite, since at most $d^n$ fillings occur for $n>0$, and at $n=0$ its unique member is the empty filling.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $k$ be a field, $q\in k^	imes$, $d\ge n$, and let $\mathcal F(X)=Xe$ be the right-module Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]].
