This explicitly extends the partition-content definition of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] to weak compositions, including internal zero counts; a zero count means that its label is absent. The set is finite, since at most $d^n$ fillings occur for $n>0$, and at $n=0$ its unique member is the empty filling.

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition of $n\ge0$ with
parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge1$ and conjugate partition
$\lambda'$, whose $j$-th part is the number $\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\ge j\}$
of nodes of $[\lambda]$ in column $j$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $j\ge1$ let
$$z_j(\lambda):=\#\{\,i:\lambda_i=j\,\}$$
be the multiplicity with which the positive integer $j$ occurs as a part of
$\lambda$; only finitely many $z_j$ are nonzero.

- $\lambda$ is **$p$-regular** when every positive part of $\lambda$ occurs
  fewer than $p$ times, that is, when $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for every $j\ge1$.
- $\lambda$ is **$p$-restricted** when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<p$ for every
  $i\ge1$, where the sequence is padded by the trailing zeros
  $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>k$.

Both conditions are finite families of inequalities. For $i>k$ one has
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}=0<p$, so the restrictedness condition is the finite
list for $1\le i\le k$. The empty partition $\varnothing\vdash0$ has no parts
and $k=0$, so $z_j(\varnothing)=0<p$ and $0-0=0<p$ for every $j,i\ge1$: it is
simultaneously $p$-regular and $p$-restricted for every prime $p$.

The two conditions are exchanged by conjugation: **$\lambda$ is $p$-restricted
if and only if $\lambda'$ is $p$-regular.** The number of columns of $[\lambda]$
of height exactly $i$ is the difference $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ of consecutive
parts, and these heights are precisely the parts of $\lambda'$, so the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$; the
stated equivalence compares the same integers with $p$.

The names record two genuinely different label conventions used later on this
page: James's modular simple modules $D^\lambda$ are labelled by **$p$-regular**
$\lambda$. Dual Specht modules themselves are defined for every partition;
their simple heads give the **$p$-restricted** labelling of simple modules,
related to the first convention by transposition and a sign twist. Neither
class of partitions contains the other in general.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $F$ be a
field of characteristic $p$. Let $\beta_F$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form on $M^\lambda_F=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, with
orthonormal tabloid basis, and let
$$S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad R^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F\cap(S^\lambda_F)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F/R^\lambda_F,$$
where $V^{\perp}=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]],
[[thm-james-submodule-theorem-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Let $G_\lambda$ be
the Gram matrix of the integral tabloid form in the standard-polytabloid
basis of the integral Specht lattice $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, and let
$g_\lambda$ be the positive greatest common divisor of its entries
([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]],
[[lem-specht-gram-gcd-detects-p-regularity]]). Write $G_\lambda\bmod p$ for
the entrywise image of $G_\lambda$ in $F$, a matrix with entries in $F$.
Then:

1. **Vanishing criterion.**
   $$D^\lambda_F=0\iff p\mid G_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j \iff p\mid g_\lambda\iff\lambda\text{ is not }p\text{-regular},$$
   and equivalently $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ if and only if $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for
   every $j\ge1$, where $z_j(\lambda)$ is the number of parts of $\lambda$
   equal to $j$.
2. **Dimension.** $\dim_FD^\lambda_F=\operatorname{rank}_F(G_\lambda\bmod p)$;
   this dimension is determined by $\lambda$ and $p$ alone, and it is
   positive exactly when $\lambda$ is $p$-regular.
3. **Structure when nonzero.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then
   $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ is the simple, self-dual and absolutely irreducible
   head of $S^\lambda_F$, and $R^\lambda_F$ is the unique maximal submodule
   of $S^\lambda_F$, equal to the module radical
   $\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_F)$.

For the $k$ of a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$,
$D^\lambda_k$ is the modular Specht quotient $D^\lambda$ of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], so the criterion above
decides for which $\lambda$ that quotient vanishes. No simplicity of
$S^\lambda_F$ itself is asserted.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ have characteristic $p>0$, let $N\ge2$, and let $\mu=(\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge\mu_N\ge0)$ be a polynomial highest weight. Let $L_N(\mu)$ be the nonzero Schur Weyl-cell simple at $q=1$, regarded as a left module by star, with its canonical highest vector $v$. Put $a_i=\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}$. For every $1\le r\le s<N$, define $B(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^j a_t$ and $C(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^{j-1}a_t$, reduced modulo $p$ for zero tests. A matching is an injection $d$ with $x\le d(x)$; it need not preserve order between different sources. Call $J\subseteq(r,s]$ essential when no $t<u$ outside $J$ in $[r,s+1]$ admits a zero-$B$ matching $\{t\}\cup(J\cap(t,u))\to[t,u)$. Write $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$ for the number of essential sets.

The vectors $T_{r,s}(J)v$ constructed by the explicit integral coefficient recursion in the proof, indexed by essential $J$, form a basis of $L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha_r-\cdots-\alpha_s}$. In particular this weight-space dimension is $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, including dimension zero. The construction has integer-polynomial coefficients, and its positive-word pivots remain valid in every field of characteristic $p$.

Define a root $x$ to be normal in $[x,y]$ when $a_x\ne0$ and its demands $m>x$ with $B(x,m)=0$ admit an injection $z$ satisfying $x<z(m)\le m$ and $B(z(m),m)=0$. If $r$ is not normal set $\nu_a(r,s)=0$; otherwise let it be the number of $x\in[r,s]$ normal in $[x,s]$ with $C(r,x)=0$. Set $\varepsilon'_a(r,t)=\varepsilon_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$, where only coordinate $t$ is increased by one. Then, as ordinary integers,
$$\varepsilon_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^s\varepsilon'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s).$$
No restrictedness condition is imposed on $\mu$ or on the shifted auxiliary highest weights.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

For $H\le G$, restriction forgets from $\mathbb Z[G]$ to $\mathbb Z[H]$. For a left $H$-module $M$, set $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=\mathbb Z[G]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[H]}M$ and $\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z[H]}(\mathbb Z[G],M)$, with $G$ acting on the latter by $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$.

derivations.claim: Use the actual $q=1$ Schur Weyl-cell simple $L_N(\mu)$, $\mu$ dominant polynomial, converted from right to left by star. Its highest vector $v$ has weight $\mu$ and norm $1$. The local lemma [F3] proves from the tensorword endomorphism realization that negative coefficient operators span each weight space, positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector, and integral cut-root words span every grade whose simple-root coefficients are $0$ or $1$. It also proves the complete essential-subset basis and the dimension formula $\dim L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha(r,s)}=\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, $a_j=\mu_j-\mu_{j+1}$. The local lemma [F3] also proves for every dominant $a$ and every interval, by finite matching/path/stack bijections and finite triangular matrix inversion, $\varepsilon_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^s\varepsilon'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s)$, where $\varepsilon'_a(r,t)=\varepsilon_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$. These are actual proved local inputs, including all zero dimensions and arbitrary nonrestricted auxiliary weights.

We spell out a further modular consequence of the same foundation to close the algebraic support seam. Let $\Gamma$ be a deficit with each simple-root coefficient $0$ or $1$, with disconnected support $\Gamma=\delta+\zeta$ separated by at least one zero coefficient. Take the first component $\delta$ entirely inside the Levi on the first $N-1$ coordinates. Every negative cut word of grade $\Gamma$ factors uniquely into a $\delta$-word and a $\zeta$-word, since no root crossing a missing simple root can occur; the two groups commute. Every positive coefficient word of grade $\Gamma$ similarly factors. All positive/negative cross commutators between the separated groups vanish. Consequently the matrix of highest coefficients at $\Gamma$ is the tensor product of the two separate coefficient matrices at $\delta$ and $\zeta$: for positive tests $e,e'$ and negative words $f,f'$, $\operatorname{highest}(ee'ff'v)=\operatorname{highest}(efv)\operatorname{highest}(e'f'v)$. The rightmost separated test/word leaves the Cartan coordinates of the other interval unchanged, since the intervals are nonadjacent; this verifies the displayed equality even though $f'fv$ has shifted weight.

Choose bases $f_av$ and $f'_bv$ of the separate images. Positive detection yields positive linear-combination tests $e_a$ and $e'_b$ with $e_af_cv=\delta_{ac}v$, $e'_bf'_dv=\delta_{bd}v$, by finite matrix inversion over the field. Thus the products $f_af'_bv$ are independent, since $e_ae'_b$ tests detect their coefficients; they span by the preceding factorization. On the entire weight space at $\Gamma$ the operator $P_\delta=\sum_a f_ae_a$ is the identity: applied to $f_cf'_bv$, its cross commutations give $f_cf'_bv$. Every $e_a$ is a positive Levi coefficient word of nonzero weight $\delta$, and every $f_a$ is a negative Levi coefficient word. This argument proves the identity on arbitrary entangled linear combinations, not only pure products. If a separate image is zero, the full weight space is zero and cannot supply a primitive vector.

Now let $M_0\subset M_1$ be consecutive terms of a finite composition series of the first level, and choose $x\in M_1$ representing the highest vector of a simple factor, of full deficit $\Gamma$. Positive Levi operators of nonzero weight send $x$ into $M_0$, because they annihilate its highest class. If $\Gamma$ had a disconnected initial component $\delta$, the identity $P_\delta x=x$ would put $x$ into $M_0$: $e_ax\in M_0$ and $f_a$ preserve $M_0$. This is impossible. Hence any primitive factor vector of binary deficit ending at the last simple root has support a single terminal interval. This is the disconnected-root primitive exclusion, proved here, without a characteristic-zero PBW theorem or a pure-product assumption for $x$.

Suppose $\mu_N=0$ and let $l=N-1$. Define the first level $M$ as the sum of weight spaces of $L_N(\mu)$ whose last diagonal coordinate is $1$. It is a polynomial Schur/$\mathrm{GL}_{N-1}$ module of degree $|\mu|-1$; the Levi preserves that coordinate. Put $ eta_i=\alpha_i+\cdots+\alpha_l$. For any $i$ write $
u_i=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{N-1})-\epsilon_i$, as a weight, and write $d_i=\dim L_N(\mu)_{\mu- eta_i}$, $b_u=[M:L_{N-1}(
u_u)]$ when $
u_u$ is dominant, and $b_u=0$ otherwise. Dominance of $
u_u$ is equivalent to $a_u>0$. No modular restriction condition is imposed on a dominant $
u_u$. In particular non-$p$-restricted factors still contribute to all character equations below.

A simple factor contributing to the $
u_i$ weight must have highest weight $\eta$ dominating $
u_i$. The standard Schur cell simples have unique highest vector, all other weights dominated by it, and cover all simple Schur modules by the cellular regular-module argument. Thus this statement applies to every factor over every field. Lift $\eta$ by appending the last coordinate $1$, and let $\Gamma=\mu-(\eta,1)$. Since $\eta$ is a weight of the first level, $\Gamma$ is a nonnegative integral combination of simple roots; since $\eta$ dominates $
u_i$, $ eta_i-\Gamma$ is a nonnegative integral combination of Levi roots. Consequently $\Gamma_j=0$ for $j<i$, $\Gamma_j\in\{0,1\}$ for $i\le j<l$, and $\Gamma_l=1$. The support exclusion just proved forces $\Gamma= eta_u$ for some $u\ge i$. Thus $\eta=
u_u$ and $
u_u$ must be dominant. Only these terminal labels can contribute to this character equation; no stronger assertion about the other first-level factors is needed.

Weight-space dimensions are additive on a composition series. Indeed the actual weight idempotents give direct projections, so taking a fixed torus weight is exact. The own highest weight of $L_{N-1}(
u_i)$, when defined, has dimension $1$. Thus $d_i=b_i+\sum_{u>i}b_ua_{iu}$, $a_{iu}=\dim L_{N-1}(
u_u)_{
u_i}$. For an invalid $
u_u$ its term is omitted. The lower weight deficit is $
u_u-
u_i=\epsilon_i-\epsilon_u=\alpha_i+\cdots+\alpha_{u-1}$. The fundamental coordinates of $
u_u$ on that interval are $a_i,\ldots,a_{u-2},a_{u-1}+1$. Any altered coordinate at $u$ is outside the interval and has no effect on the local formulas. The proved interval-basis theorem therefore gives $d_i=\varepsilon_a(i,l)$, $a_{iu}=\varepsilon'_a(i,u-1)$. This is valid for every legitimate dominant $
u_u$, including those not $p$-restricted. When $a_u=0$, $
u_u$ is nondominant and $b_u=0$; also $
u_a(u,l)=0$ because its root is not normal.

Substitute these dimensions into the character equation and compare it with the local recurrence of [F3] at $(i,l)$: $\varepsilon_a(i,l)=b_i+\sum_{u>i}b_u\varepsilon'_a(i,u-1)$, $\varepsilon_a(i,l)=
u_a(i,l)+\sum_{u>i}
u_a(u,l)\varepsilon'_a(i,u-1)$. Starting at $i=l$ and proceeding downwards proves $b_i=
u_a(i,l)$ for all $i$. This is finite integer reverse substitution, never reduction of the character multiplicities modulo $p$. The rank is $N-1$, unrelated to the prime except in the $B,C$ zero tests.

The local lemma [F3] uses only the infinite purely transcendental extension $K=F(t)$ for polynomial identities and Gaussian elimination. Its scalar-extension argument is reversible: all cut/raising matrices have entries in $F$, hence their finite ranks and kernels preserve extension; its essential labels and pivot tests yield bases over $F$ itself. Schur cell simples remain simple under every field extension by the cellular rank-one action and their nonzero form. Extending a finite Schur composition series thus retains the simple factors and their labels, so the integers $b_i$ computed over $K$ are exactly those over $F$. The first-level weight subspace commutes with extension because it is the image of a finite sum of weight idempotents. Neither an algebraic closure nor an assumption that the original field is infinite is used. All nil/zero-weight cases remain in the equations.

Let $\lambda$ be $p$-regular, $\lambda\ne(n)$, put $N=n$, $\mu=\lambda'$, $\mu_N=0$. The index of $A=(j,\lambda_j)$ is $i=\lambda_j$, not $j$, and not $p$. The coordinate $a_u=\mu_u-\mu_{u+1}$ is the multiplicity of the part $u$ in $\lambda$; in particular $a_u<p$, but the preceding algebraic proof did not need that restriction. A removable $A$ is the last row of its width $i$ block, hence $j=\mu_i$.

The root normal walk based at $i$ starts with a push for $A$ and scans $u=i+1,\ldots,l$. At coordinates with $a_u=0$ the compensation walk is neutral, even when $B=C=0$: the same position supplies and consumes a compensation slot. At positive coordinates $u$, the last ordinary row $k$ of the width $u$ block gives a removable node, and $C(i,u)=u-i+\sum_{t=i}^{u-1}a_t=u-\lambda_j+j-k$. Thus $C(i,u)=0$ is exactly the removable node's residue equal to $A$'s residue. The first ordinary row $k$ of the width $u$ block has an addable node in column $u+1$, and $B(i,u)=u-i+\sum_{t=i}^{u}a_t=u-\lambda_j+j-k+1$. Thus $B(i,u)=0$ is exactly that addable node's residue equal to $A$'s residue. Since $0<a_u<p$ at a positive coordinate, $B=C+a_u$ shows these two events cannot occur together at that same $u$. Empty widths give only the neutral compensation case. The artificial final zero-width row also has no effect. Scanning positive $u$ in increasing order lists the ordinary corners above $A$ in the order $j-1,\ldots,1$, with a width block contributing its boundary event when the residue matches. The top extra addable node of width $\lambda_1+1$ is already the $B$ event of the width $\lambda_1$ coordinate; no boundary event is omitted.

Under transpose a removable ordinary node becomes a removable $\mu$-node of opposite residue, and an addable becomes an addable of opposite residue. The top-to-bottom $\mu$-signature following $A'$ lists exactly these above ordinary nodes in this order. The only possible equal-column lower ordinary addable node lies immediately below $A$ and has residue differing by $1$, so it is absent from this residue class. Consequently the root push/pop walk is exactly the reduced-signature stack after $A'$: push a removable $-$, pop on an addable $+$, implementing cancellation $-+$.

Earlier signature signs do not change whether $A'$ or any later push is removed. $A$ survives precisely when no later prefix has more pops than pushes; this is exactly root normality $\sigma(i,l)$. If it survives, the final stack consists of $A$ together with those above ordinary removable nodes in $A$'s residue class whose transposes survive as normal nodes. The stack proof of [F3] identifies this final stack with $N(i,l)$, so $\nu_a(i,l)=0$ if $A$ is not normal, and $\nu_a(i,l)=1+\#\{\text{normal removable nodes strictly above }A\text{ of }A\text{'s residue}\}$ if $A$ is normal. The node count here is piecewise. It is not the unconditioned count of normal nodes weakly above $A$ when $A$ is nonnormal.

Work at $q=1$ with right Schur modules, reversing the star conversion used for the algebraic count. The Hecke presentation has $T_i^2=1$ and the symmetric-group braid relations; its standard basis $T_w$ maps bijectively to the group basis $w$, so $H(F,1,S_m)=FS_m$. Let $e$ be the weight projection of type $\omega=(1^m)$, with $\operatorname{End}_H(H)=H$ via $\rho_h(x)=hx$. The normalized semistandard map $\varphi_{ST}$ is supported from $\operatorname{type}(T)$ to $\operatorname{type}(S)$. Thus $e\varphi_{ST}e$ survives exactly when both types are $\omega$. These tableaux are ordinary standard tableaux, their defining fibers are singleton, and evaluation at $1$ gives $\varphi_{st}\mapsto m_{st}$. The higher Schur ideal corner is exactly the higher Murphy ideal, as equality of the corresponding basis spans. The projection on a Weyl cell fixes $w_T$ exactly for $\operatorname{type}(T)=\omega$. To read its right $H$ action, choose the independent fixed outer index also of type $\omega$; evaluation at $1$ then turns $\varphi_{st}\rho_h$ into $m_{st}h$ modulo the corresponding higher ideal. Hence $W^\xi e\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\xi)$ by $w_t\mapsto c_t$, with the actual same-shape Murphy action, over every field.

Choose all four indices $a,s,t,b$ standard of shape $\xi$ and type $\omega$ in the Schur cell product $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\xi(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$. Evaluate every map at $1$ in the corner. The Murphy product is $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\xi(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$, so its independent cell-product coefficient gives $B_\xi(w_s,w_t)=G_{\mathrm M,\xi}(c_s,c_t)$. The scalar is exactly $1$. Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\xi(xe,y(1-e))=B_\xi(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. Thus the Weyl decomposition $W^\xi=W^\xi e\oplus W^\xi(1-e)$ is orthogonal, and $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\xi e)=\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\xi)e$, including an identically zero corner form. The canonical shape/type $\xi$ diagonal is the projection onto $M^\xi$ and is idempotent, so the same cell-product coefficient gives canonical norm $1$; $L^\xi=W^\xi/\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}$ is nonzero simple. Projection by $e$ is exact (lift $ye$ by $xe$, and kernels are intersections fixed by $e$), so $L^\xi e\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\xi)$, including zero. At $q=1$ the unit form comparison [F2] gives $D_{\mathrm M}(\xi)\cong D^{\xi'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ when $\xi'$ is regular, and zero otherwise by the published ordinary radical criterion. These nonzero quotients are distinctly labelled group simples. This proves restricted survival locally and uses no general finite-e classification.

Take $N=m=n$ and the tensorword realization of $S(N,m)$ already proved in [F3]. Let $p$ be the sum of all actual weight projections with last coordinate $1$. Its tensorwords have exactly one occurrence of $N$. Identify their remaining ordered positions with $(F^{N-1})^{\otimes(m-1)}$. For each lower Schur orbit matrix $E_A$, define $\kappa(E_A)=E_{\operatorname{diag}(A,1)}$, where the last row and column have only their final entry $1$. On every word with one $N$ this map preserves its position and applies $E_A$ to the other positions. Consequently products are exactly the lower products, $\kappa(1)=p$, and $\kappa$ embeds $S(N-1,m-1)$ as a unital subalgebra of $pS(N,m)p$. This describes the lower Schur action on $Xp$, and for the star-converted left simple it is exactly the block-diagonal $\mathrm{GL}_{N-1}$ action used in the character calculation, because $g^{\otimes(m-1)}$ expands in $E_A$ and $\operatorname{diag}(g,1)$ acts at the unchanged $N$ position. Transpose sends $E_A$ to $E_{A^{\mathsf t}}$, so $\kappa$ respects star. The first level counted above is therefore precisely $L_N(\mu)p$, converted to the right; no source-only definition of first level is being substituted.

Let $e'$ be the lower regular-type projection $(1^{N-1})$. In this embedding $\kappa(e')=e$, the full type $(1^N)$ projection. Use the explicit coset-word map $m_\nu T_d\mapsto(\text{row of entry }j\text{ in }t^\nu d)_j$. On the regular type its jth letter is $jd^{-1}$, in right permutation notation. Consequently $\rho_h:d\mapsto hd$ changes a regular word by the corresponding label permutation $h^{-1}$, because $(hd)^{-1}=d^{-1}h^{-1}$. A lower corner element $\rho'_h$ acts by this same label permutation $h^{-1}$ on $1,\ldots,N-1$ and fixes label $N$. The orbit embedding therefore gives exactly $\rho_h$ on the full regular tensorword basis, with no extra inversion or opposite-algebra map. Thus $\kappa(\rho'_h)=\rho_h$, with the subgroup action in the right convention exactly $X\rho_h$. Consequently $(Xp)e'=Xe$ as $FS_{N-1}$-modules, with the latter the ordinary restriction of $Xe$. Apply this to $X=L_N(\mu)$. This is the complete local $q=1$ first-level/corner identity; it is independent of the held generic comparison.

Apply the exact lower projection $e'$ to a finite composition series of $L_N(\mu)p$. Each factor $L_{N-1}(\eta)$ becomes $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, proved by the lower-rank form/corner calculation of steps 14.1–15.1; it is a distinctly labelled simple when $\eta$ is restricted, and zero otherwise. Deleting repeated terms leaves a composition series of the group restriction corner. Thus the multiplicity of a restricted $\eta$ agrees exactly with its lower Schur multiplicity. Nonrestricted $\eta$ were retained in the earlier character calculation and are killed only here. For $\mu=\lambda'$, [F2] gives $L_N(\mu)e\cong D^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$. The candidate $\nu_i=(\lambda\setminus A)'$ is restricted by the regular-removal hypothesis, and its image is $D^{\lambda\setminus A}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$. Hence the desired group restriction multiplicity is $b_i$. Twisting both modules by sign preserves multiplicity because sign of $S_n$ restricts to sign of $S_{n-1}$. To match a left-module convention for the ordinary $D$ in the Statement, apply the exact inverse/star equivalence from right group modules to left ones, $g\cdot x=xg^{-1}$. It commutes with restriction and sign twisting and preserves composition series. The ordinary polytabloid quotient is the same partition-labelled quotient in this convention; if the dictionary uses its contragredient realization, the induced nondegenerate invariant quotient form identifies that simple with its contragredient. Explicitly $x\mapsto(y\mapsto\beta(x,y))$ is bijective and equivariant since $\beta(gx,y)=\beta(x,g^{-1}y)$. This uses the form only after passing to the nonzero radical quotient, as in [[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]; no self-duality of a possibly degenerate Specht module is assumed. Together with the algebraic count and signature calculation, this gives both displayed cases of the theorem.

For $\lambda=(n)$ the ordinary simple is trivial and restricts trivially, so the unique removable node has multiplicity $1$. Its transposed $\mu=(1^n)$ node is normal: no subsequent same-residue addable can cancel it, and the preceding possible addable gives a $+-$ pair rather than a cancellation. There are no above ordinary removables. For $n=1$ this is the one-dimensional restriction to $S_0$; for $n=0$ the removable-node hypothesis is empty. These cases avoid requiring $\mu_N=0$ where it is false. All primes, all fields of characteristic $p$, all $p$-regular $\lambda$ and all regular removals retain the original stated scope.

The piecewise integer $\gamma(A)=\mathbf1_{A\text{ normal}}$ times the number of normal nodes weakly above $A$ has value zero off normality and is at least one on normality, since $A$ itself is counted. The preceding multiplicity and boundary proofs therefore establish both the formula and its stated equivalence over every field of characteristic $p$.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting

([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ (every field is splitting for
symmetric groups, so no algebraic closedness is needed) and let $\lambda$ be
a $p$-regular partition of $n$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]), so that $D^\lambda$ is the
simple head of the Specht module $S^\lambda_k$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). Let
$A=(j,\lambda_j)$ be a removable node of $\lambda$ whose removal
$\lambda(j)$ is again $p$-regular, and call $A$ **normal** for $\lambda$ when
the transposed node $(\lambda_j,j)$ of the $p$-restricted partition
$\lambda'$ is a normal node in the sense of
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] (this is
Kleshchev's normality; it is computed in the reduced signature of the correct
residue class of $\lambda'$). Then
$$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=0$$
if $A$ is not normal, and
$$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=1+\#\{B:\ B\ \text{is a normal removable node of }\lambda\text{ strictly above }A\text{ with }\operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$$
if $A$ is normal. Here $\operatorname{res}$ is the residue $c-r\bmod p$ and
"above" means strictly smaller row index. Equivalently, the multiplicity is the piecewise integer
$\gamma(A)=\mathbf1_{A\text{ normal}}\cdot\#\{B:B\text{ normal removable, weakly above }A,\ \operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$.
Thus $A$ is normal precisely when this piecewise multiplicity is nonzero.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $F$ have characteristic $p>0$, let $N\ge2$, and let $\mu=(\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge\mu_N\ge0)$ be a polynomial highest weight. Let $L_N(\mu)$ be the nonzero Schur Weyl-cell simple at $q=1$, regarded as a left module by star, with its canonical highest vector $v$. Put $a_i=\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}$. For every $1\le r\le s<N$, define $B(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^j a_t$ and $C(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^{j-1}a_t$, reduced modulo $p$ for zero tests. A matching is an injection $d$ with $x\le d(x)$; it need not preserve order between different sources. Call $J\subseteq(r,s]$ essential when no $t<u$ outside $J$ in $[r,s+1]$ admits a zero-$B$ matching $\{t\}\cup(J\cap(t,u))\to[t,u)$. Write $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$ for the number of essential sets.

The vectors $T_{r,s}(J)v$ constructed by the explicit integral coefficient recursion in the proof, indexed by essential $J$, form a basis of $L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha_r-\cdots-\alpha_s}$. In particular this weight-space dimension is $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, including dimension zero. The construction has integer-polynomial coefficients, and its positive-word pivots remain valid in every field of characteristic $p$.

Define a root $x$ to be normal in $[x,y]$ when $a_x\ne0$ and its demands $m>x$ with $B(x,m)=0$ admit an injection $z$ satisfying $x<z(m)\le m$ and $B(z(m),m)=0$. If $r$ is not normal set $\nu_a(r,s)=0$; otherwise let it be the number of $x\in[r,s]$ normal in $[x,s]$ with $C(r,x)=0$. Set $\varepsilon'_a(r,t)=\varepsilon_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$, where only coordinate $t$ is increased by one. Then, as ordinary integers,
$$\varepsilon_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^s\varepsilon'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s).$$
No restrictedness condition is imposed on $\mu$ or on the shifted auxiliary highest weights.

Thus $A$ is normal precisely when this piecewise multiplicity is nonzero.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $n\ge1$. (a) The elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ act diagonally in the Young
basis of the previous item: for every standard tableau $T$ of size $n$ and
every $k$, $X_kv_T=c_T(k)v_T$, and the joint eigenspaces are
one-dimensional, indexed by the standard tableaux. (b) A vector
$\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$ occurs as the joint eigenvalue vector
of a $v_T$, equivalently $\alpha=\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ for a standard
tableau $T$, if and only if: (1) $a_1=0$; (2) for every $q>1$ at least one of
$a_q-1,a_q+1$ occurs among $a_1,\dots,a_{q-1}$; (3) if $a_p=a_q$ with $p<q$,
then both $a_p-1$ and $a_p+1$ occur among $a_{p+1},\dots,a_{q-1}$. The
association $T\mapsto\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ is a bijection from the standard
tableaux of size $n$ onto this set.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.
