No converse is asserted: the statement does not claim that a node whose multiplicity is the counted value must be conormal, only the two conditional values proved in step 2.1.

derivations.claim: For $d>0$ take $N=d+1$, pad $\mu$ by zeros, set $a_j=\mu_j-\mu_{j+1}$, let $L=L_N(\mu)$ be the actual Schur simple, $V=F^N$, and $M=V\otimes L$. Tensor coefficient operators are the actual polynomial Schur operators of degree $d+1$, obtained by multiplying the two polynomial matrix actions. This works over finite fields without replacing coefficient actions by evaluated group elements. The case $d=0$ is treated below.

Here is the local component identity used below. If a binary root deficit has separated connected components (a zero simple-root coefficient between consecutive components), its negative words split into products supported on those components. All cross-component positive and negative root operators commute, and their Cartan characters on the other component are unchanged: their simple-root supports are nonadjacent. Move the positive words past the other components and evaluate their highest coefficients one component at a time. The positive/negative coefficient matrix is consequently the tensor product of the component matrices. Negative-word spanning and positive detection identify its quotient by the common positive-test kernel with the actual simple weight space. Hence this weight space is the tensor product of the component quotients, including when one is zero. This proves the assertion directly from coefficient words; it does not assume a tensor-product decomposition of the whole simple module.

In particular fix one component $\delta$. Choose a negative basis $f_1v,\ldots,f_tv$ of its quotient and positive tests $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ dual to it. They are finite linear combinations of actual coefficient words, with coefficients in $F$; their existence follows from positive detection and ordinary finite-dimensional linear algebra. Then $P_\delta=\sum_{h=1}^t f_he_h$ is the identity on every binary weight space having this component and any separated other components. The same tests apply because the other components change none of the Cartan data of $\delta$. If $t=0$, these weight spaces are zero. This is an identity of coefficient operators on those spaces, so it descends to subquotients.

Write $\xi_i=\mu+\epsilon_i$. Suppose a simple composition factor with highest weight $\eta$ contributes at $\xi_i$. All weights of $M$ are at most $\mu+\epsilon_1$, and weights of that factor are at most $\eta$. Thus $\xi_i\le\eta\le\mu+\epsilon_1.$

The deficit $\Gamma=\mu+\epsilon_1-\eta$ has simple-root coefficients $0$ or $1$ in positions $1,\ldots,i-1$ and zero elsewhere. On a tensor summand $v_j\otimes L_{\eta-\epsilon_j}$ the deficit in $L$ is $\Gamma-(\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_{j-1}).$

It must be nonnegative. Consequently every possible label $j$ lies before the first missing coefficient in $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$ has a component $\delta$ after that first gap, every positive or negative coefficient word supported on $\delta$ fixes the $V$ factor (its nonconstant terms annihilate each of these labels). Its action on this tensor weight is therefore purely its action on $L$. The preceding $P_\delta$ is the identity on the entire weight $M_\eta$, not just on individual tensor summands.

Choose a composition series and a lift $x\in M_\eta$ of the nonzero highest vector of the proposed factor in its series quotient. Each $e_hx$ lies in the preceding submodule because it has strictly higher weight, and each $f_h$ preserves that submodule. But $P_\delta x=x$ would then place $x$ in it, a contradiction. If the component quotient is zero there was no such tensor weight to start with. Thus $\Gamma$ has no later component. Its only possible nonzero coefficients form one initial interval, and $\eta=\mu+\epsilon_u\quad\text{for some }u\le i.$
This excludes only highest weights of factors contributing to $\xi_i$. It asserts nothing about distant tensor factors.
Since every weight of $L$ is at most $\mu$, $M_{\xi_i}=\bigoplus_{j\le i}v_j\otimes L_{\mu+\epsilon_i-\epsilon_j},\qquad d_i:=\dim M_{\xi_i}=1+\sum_{j<i}E_a(j,i-1).$

Let $b_u$ be the actual composition multiplicity of $L_N(\mu+\epsilon_u)$ in $M$ when that weight is dominant; set $b_u=0$ otherwise. No restrictedness condition is imposed on these auxiliary factors. The support lemma and the one-dimensional highest spaces give $d_i=b_i+\sum_{u<i}b_uE_{a+\omega_u}(u,i-1).$ (equation C).

Indeed $\mu+\epsilon_u-\xi_i=\alpha_u+\cdots+\alpha_{i-1}$. On this interval the fundamental coordinates of the dominant weight $\mu+\epsilon_u$ are those of $a$ with its first coordinate $u$ increased by one; the coordinate $u-1$ changed by minus one lies outside the interval. Nondominant rows have multiplicity zero, so their formal summands cause no alteration of (C).

For completeness the weight-dimension symmetry needed here is local. Permutation matrices permute the integer weight spaces of $L$. Hence its lowest weight is $w_0\mu$, its space is one dimensional, and every weight lies between $w_0\mu$ and $\mu$. The contragredient dual twisted by $\det^d$ is a polynomial simple of highest weight $\mu^*=(d-\mu_N,\ldots,d-\mu_1).$

One can verify polynomiality without a rational-module classification theorem. The tensorword Schur algebra acts faithfully on $V^{\otimes d}$; its regular module embeds in a finite direct sum of copies of this tensor space by its action on a basis. Thus every simple is a subquotient of copies of this tensor space. Duality and the twist make it a subquotient of $(V^*\otimes\det)^{\otimes d}$; the explicit exterior-complement pairing gives $V^*\otimes\det\cong\bigwedge^{N-1}V$ over every field. It is therefore polynomial. Positive and negative coefficients interchange under duality, so the highest weight just identified determines the same actual Schur simple as in the accepted foundation. These statements are coefficient identities; over a finite field they can equivalently be checked over $F(t)$ and descended as the identical finite matrices.
Put $\bar a_t=a_{N-t}$. Duality reverses roots and preserves weight dimensions, yielding $E_a(j,i-1)=E_{\bar a}(N-i+1,N-j).$

This argument applies also to any dominant shifted weight. In particular the first-coordinate shift at $u$ becomes the final-coordinate shift at $N-u$ on the reversed interval. No restriction on its fundamental coordinates is needed.

Reverse the indices: $r=N-i+1$, $\bar b_r=b_i$, $\bar d_r=d_i$. On indices $1,\ldots,N$, let the strictly upper triangular matrices be $A[r,v]=\nu'_{\bar a}(r,v-1),\qquad B[r,v]=E'_{\bar a}(r,v-1)\quad(r<v).$

For $r<v$, apply the accepted recurrence to $[r,v-1]$ after increasing coordinate $v-1$. Every earlier interval $[r,u-1]$ with $u<v$ is unaffected, while the tail normal count is shifted at $v-1$. Thus $B[r,v]=A[r,v]+\sum_{r<u<v}B[r,u]A[u,v]$, or $B=A+BA$. Hence $(I+B)(I-A)=I$. Since these are finite integer matrices, the inverse is two-sided and $(I+B)^{-1}=I-A$. Equivalently, the supplier's first-cut recurrence gives $B=A+AB$ and $I+B=I+A+\cdots+A^{N-1}$.
Let $H_r=\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)$, with $H_N=0$. Applying the accepted recurrence separately for every endpoint and summing gives $\bar d=\mathbf1+(I+B)H.$

Opposition turns (C) into $\bar d=(I+B)\bar b$. Multiplication by $I-A$ gives, as ordinary integers, $b_i=1+\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\bigl(\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)-\nu'_{\bar a}(r,s)\bigr),\qquad r=N-i+1.$ (equation D).
This is finite nilpotent matrix arithmetic. It neither divides in $F$ nor replaces a composition multiplicity by a residue in $F$.

Use the accepted normal-stack interpretation; every coordinate and $B,C$ equality tested in this paragraph and the endpoint analysis is modulo $p$, whereas stack heights are ordinary integers. Write $\sigma(r,t)$ for its alive indicator and put $\sigma(r,r-1)=1$. For every dominant coordinate array $\lambda$, $\nu_\lambda(r,s)-\nu'_\lambda(r,s)=\sigma(r,s-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}\right).$ (equation E).

If killed before the final step, both counts are zero. Otherwise let its current height be $h\ge1$. The endpoint shift keeps $C(r,s)$ fixed and replaces $B$ and $\lambda_s$ by $B+1$ and $\lambda_s+1$. If $B=-1$ it creates a pop and lowers the count by one; when $\lambda_s=-1$, the unshifted step instead pushes and the shifted zero-coordinate step is neutral, with the same difference. If $B=0$ it removes a pop and increases the count by one; when $\lambda_s=0$, the old step is neutral and the new step pushes, again with that difference. For other $B$ neither change alters the count. If a pop removes the initial root, its new count is zero, still $h-1=0$. At $s=r$ the two counts are $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r\ne0}$ and $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r+1\ne0}$, giving the same formula. These alternatives are exhaustive and valid for $p=2$.

Fix an actual addable row $i$ and put $R_j=\mu_j+1-j$, $\rho=R_i\pmod p$. If $i>1$, addability means $a_{i-1}>0$. Since $\mu$ is restricted, $0<a_{i-1}<p$; the reversed root therefore starts alive. For $r=N-i+1$, $s=N-j$, direct substitution gives $B_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_j-R_i-1,\qquad C_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_{j+1}-R_i.$

Thus the two indicators in (E) respectively detect an addable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$ and a removable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$. The normal stack processes the boundary in reverse order, starting with the chosen $+$ in row $i$. At step $j$ its $C=0$ push corresponds to the plus in row $j+1$, and its $B=0$ pop to the minus in row $j$. The top-row plus is a pending final event. This reversal is exactly the stack evaluation of $-+$ cancellation: in a reverse scan, a minus cancels the most recently encountered plus.
Here is the precise check at flat row blocks and at the endpoints. Let $D_s=1+\sum_{t=r}^s\sigma(r,t-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=0}\right).$

While the chosen root remains alive, $D_s$ is its current normal-stack height plus the pending indicator $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}$, where $j=N-s$. At the initial step the removable event $B(r,r)=0$ cannot occur since $0<a_{i-1}<p$, and this identity follows immediately. At each subsequent live step the change in height is $\mathbf1_{C(r,s)=0}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}.$

For $a_j\ne0$ these are disjoint push/pop events. For $a_j=0$ the indicators are equal and the step is neutral, as required by the actual stack. Subtracting this height change from the change in $D_s$ gives $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}-\mathbf1_{R_{j+1}=R_i},$

which replaces the previous pending indicator by the next. This proves the invariant by induction, including flat blocks. Equivalently, at each flat boundary $a_j=0$, the virtual removable sign in row $j$ and virtual addable sign in row $j+1$ have the same residue and form an adjacent $-+$ pair in the selected-residue row-boundary word. Deleting these pairs restores exactly the actual boundary word. By signature confluence their insertion or deletion has no effect on the surviving actual nodes. The chosen node is an actual addable, so it is never among the virtual pairs.

If the initial root is killed, its preceding height was one, the current event is $B=0$, and $B=-1$ is false. The pending indicator after the step is zero. Thus $D_s=0$, and every later term is zero because the alive indicator remains zero. In the reversed boundary scan, killing the initial plus likewise means that the chosen node is canceled; later pluses above it cannot revive it. At the last step the pending indicator is the actual addable top-row plus. We have therefore evaluated exactly the reverse scan of the prefix ending at the chosen node. A minus below this prefix cannot cancel a plus in it under top-to-bottom $-+$ cancellation; the conormal decisions for this prefix agree with those in the entire signature.

Consequently (D) is zero precisely when the chosen plus is canceled. If it survives, (D) is the number of surviving pluses of residue $\rho$ in the prefix, namely the number of conormal nodes weakly above $B$. For $i=1$, (D) is $b_1=1$: the top plus survives and it is the only node weakly above itself. For completeness, a nondominant row $i>1$ has $a_{i-1}=0$; the first endpoint difference is $-1$, killing the virtual initial unit and all later differences, so (D) gives zero as required by (C). These rows were not silently discarded during the integer inversion.
Let $\omega=(1^N)$ be the regular degree-$N$ weight. Then $M_\omega=\bigoplus_{j=1}^N v_j\otimes L_{\omega-\epsilon_j}.$

Let $G=\mathfrak S_N$, $H=\mathfrak S_d$ fixing label $N$, and $W=L_{\omega-\epsilon_N}$. The accepted local $q=1$ corner/form calculation applies to degree $d$ and rank $N$ with regular weight $(1^d,0)$: its surviving semistandard indices are precisely standard tableaux, and evaluating the corner at $1$ gives the same Murphy basis and scalar-$1$ form, regardless of the unused last label. Its radical-corner equality therefore makes $W$ the left group module $D(\mu)$. To fix the action convention, the supplier's right corner element $\rho_h$ permutes tensorword labels by $h^{-1}$; star conversion makes left $g$ act by right $g^{-1}$, hence by label permutation $g$. The same conversion in the degree-$N$ corner gives the output action. Thus the output regular-corner action is ordinary permutation of labels: on tensorwords the corresponding orbit matrix is exactly that label permutation. Since these are identities in the actual tensorword Schur algebra, the same equality holds on $M$; it does not depend on evaluated permutation matrices spanning the Schur algebra.
The explicit map $F[G]\otimes_{F[H]}W\longrightarrow M_\omega,\qquad g\otimes w\longmapsto g(v_N\otimes w)$.

is well defined and $G$-equivariant. Left cosets of $H$ correspond to the image label $gN$, and their summands map bijectively to the displayed summands of $M_\omega$. It is therefore an isomorphism. This proves $M_\omega\cong\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathfrak S_d}^{\mathfrak S_{d+1}}D(\mu)$, without Frobenius reciprocity or an adjunction multiplicity assertion.

Corner projection is exact. Each Schur composition factor $L_N(\eta)$ projects to the distinct restricted group simple $D(\eta)$ if $\eta$ is restricted, and to zero otherwise, by the accepted local form/radical and ordinary-group survival proof. Hence for a restricted $\mu+B=\mu+\epsilon_i$, its total induction multiplicity is exactly $b_i$. Nonrestricted near factors were kept until this exact projection. Distant factors were never excluded; distinct surviving labels ensure that they cannot change this particular count. When $d=0$, the single degree-one tensor/corner gives the unique plus and multiplicity one directly.

The generalized Jucys--Murphy induction summands give a direct decomposition of total induction. For the ordinary group elements $L_k=\sum_{j<k}(j,k)$, induction by inserting the letter $n$ into a cycle gives the integral identity $\prod_{k=1}^n(t+L_k)=\sum_{g\in\mathfrak S_n}t^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g.$

The factor $t$ makes $n$ a new fixed point; each transposition $(j,n)$ inserts $n$ at the uniquely specified place in the cycle containing $j$. These alternatives are disjoint and exhaust the permutations. Coefficients on the right are class sums, so all coefficients of $Q_n(t)=\prod_{k=1}^n(t-L_k)$ are central over the integers and every field.

The published [[thm-jucys-murphy-joint-spectrum-is-the-set-of-tableau-content-vectors]] says that $Q_n(t)$ acts on the complex ordinary Specht module of shape $\lambda$ as $\prod_{A\in\lambda}(t-\operatorname{res}_{\mathbb Z}(A))$. The ordinary integral Specht lattice has the free polytabloid basis provided by the accepted integral bridge. The operator equality has integer matrices on that lattice; its validity after scalar extension to $\mathbb C$ therefore implies its validity over $\mathbb Z$. Reducing and taking its radical quotient proves the same content scalar on ordinary $D^\lambda$ over every field. The accepted signed-conjugate dictionary sends each $L_k$ to $-L_k$ under the sign twist, and transpose negates contents. Hence $Q_n(t)$ acts on restricted $D(\lambda)=D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ by the content polynomial of $\lambda$. This use of the published complex spectrum is an integral operator-identity descent; none of the multiplicity inversion uses characteristic-zero composition counts or semisimplicity.

Let $\alpha$ be the multiset of residues of $\mu$. The exact central content polynomial on $D(\mu)$ and the central CRT description of the content sums give $e_\alpha^{(d)}D(\mu)=D(\mu)$; this requires no primitive-block assertion. For clarity the functor idempotent $e=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,h}$ implies the following test on $F_hD(\mu)=F\mathfrak S_{d+1}e\otimes_{F\mathfrak S_d}D(\mu)$. On its generating subspace $e\otimes D(\mu)$, the first-$d$ content polynomial has exactly the scalar for $\mu$, and $L_{d+1}-h$ is nilpotent. These operators commute and $(L_{d+1}-h)^m e=0$ for a fixed primary exponent $m$. A coefficient $z$ of $Q_{d+1}(t)-(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$ is central by the integral identity. On $e\otimes w$ it is the corresponding scalar coefficient of $Q_\mu(t)$ times $h-L_{d+1}$: balance the first-$d$ central coefficient across $e$ into $w$. Centrality lets this same calculation iterate, so $z^m(e\otimes w)=0$. Since the whole module is generated by these vectors and $z$ commutes with every group translate, $z^m$ is zero on the whole module. On a simple factor a nilpotent central endomorphism is zero, since every nonzero simple-module endomorphism is invertible. Thus every factor in this summand has content polynomial $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$.

Distinct residues give distinct polynomials: $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)-(t-k)Q_\mu(t)=(k-h)Q_\mu(t)\ne0$ for $h\ne k$. The content polynomial of $\mu+B$ appends exactly the residue of $B$. Its factors therefore occur only in the corresponding residue summand. The total multiplicity computed above is exactly the multiplicity in $F_iD(\mu)$ required by the target. This argument does not use primitivity or exhaustiveness of any content-block idempotent.
Transpose preserves boundary types. Literally $(\mu\cup B)'=\mu'\cup B^{\mathsf t},\qquad(\mu\setminus A)'=\mu'\setminus A^{\mathsf t}.$

It sends an addable node to an addable node and a removable node to a removable node; it negates the residue. The appropriate boundary reading order is reversed when transporting the signature convention. It does not exchange addable and removable sets. The proof above needs no claimed equality of induction and restriction multiplicities and no transpose transfer of a restriction count.

The finite character inversion, boundary-stack calculation, exact induction corner and residue allocation just proved identify the stated multiplicity with zero off conormality and with the conormal weak-above count on conormality. Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted
partition of $d\ge1$; write $D(\mu)$ for the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
Let $A_i$ denote the good $i$-node of $\mu$, for those
$i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i),$$
a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules: distinct residues give
distinct summands. The sum runs over the residues $i$ with
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, one good node per such residue; the completely
reducible special case (the restriction is semisimple if and only if every
normal node is good, Kleshchev II Theorem 0.6) is a separate statement and is
not asserted here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $A$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ such that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
is again $p$-restricted; let $D(\mu)$ be the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$ in the dual-Specht (cellular) convention, so that
$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]],
[[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]), and let
$E_i$ be the residue-summand functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $A$ is not a normal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B:\ B\ \text{normal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly below }A\}$$
(counting $A$ itself) if $A$ is normal. The corresponding
Specht-to-restriction Hom criterion (Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5, equivalently
Kleshchev II Theorem 0.4) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $A$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ such that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
is again $p$-restricted; let $D(\mu)$ be the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by

([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]],

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

boundaries.evidence: Multiplicity zero does not occur under the hypothesis: by step 2.1 the multiplicity is ε_i(μ) ≥ 1; the good-node factor must occur, which is part of the content of the theorem.
The minimal case ε_i(μ) = 1 gives multiplicity 1 with simple socle and head D(ν); step 1.1 covers the single summand and step 2.1 the count.

p = 2 is included by the recorded source statement [F1] and by the duality argument of step 2.2, which uses only antipode invariance and self-duality; the statement imposes no characteristic restriction.
Socle and head are exactly the two endpoints of E_iD(μ); steps 1.1 and 2.2 compute them as D(ν), and step 3.1 records that the middle Loewy layers are left unspecified.
No choice is made: the good node of each residue is unique (step 1.1) and the module E_iD(μ) is fixed by the idempotent decomposition of step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The theorem states that the good node gives a simple socle and head with total multiplicity ε_i(μ); it is not a biconditional, so there is no forward implication to check.
No converse is asserted: the theorem does not claim that a simple socle of E_iD(μ) forces A to be the good node, only the implication from the good node to the socle and head.

derivations.claim: Socle. By [F5] the socle of $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)=\bigoplus_jE_jD(\mu)$ is $\bigoplus_j\operatorname{soc}(E_jD(\mu))$. By [F1] the socle of the restriction is the multiplicity-free sum of the $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ over the good nodes, and by [F2] each summand $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ lies in $E_jD(\mu)$ with its residue $j$; since a nonzero submodule of $E_jD(\mu)$ cannot lie in $\bigoplus_{l\ne j}E_lD(\mu)$ by the directness of the sum, the $j$-summand of the socle is exactly the single simple module $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ and $\operatorname{soc}(E_jD(\mu))=D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ is simple. For $j=i$ this gives $\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))=D(\mu\setminus A)=D(\nu)$.

Multiplicity. Applying the normal-node theorem [F3] with $X=A$: since $A$ is a normal $i$-node, $[E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)]$ is the number of normal $i$-nodes of $\mu$ weakly below $A$ counting $A$; by [F6] this is $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$.

Head. By [F4] the module $E_iD(\mu)$ is self-dual; by [F5] its head is the dual of its socle, $\operatorname{hd}(E_iD(\mu))\cong(\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu)))^*$, which by step 1.1 is $D(
u)^*\cong D(
u)$ because $D(
u)$ is self-dual by [F4]. Hence the head is simple and isomorphic to $D(
u)$.

Conclusion. Step 1.1 gives simple socle $D(
u)$, step 2.1 the total multiplicity $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ of $D(
u)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$, and step 2.2 simple head $D(
u)$. The additional normal-node composition factors of [F3] may occur in the middle Loewy layers; the statement asserts only the endpoints and the total multiplicity, and no graded shift is displayed before the Hecke/KLR bridge.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of weak compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$; zero parts are allowed and give empty rows). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

For a weak composition $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$, define $T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ to be the fillings of $[\lambda]$ by $1,\ldots,d$ with exactly $\mu_i$ entries equal to $i$, weakly increasing rows and strictly increasing columns. Put $T_0(\lambda)= igcup_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ and $K_{\lambda\mu}:=|T_0(\lambda,\mu)|$. This explicitly extends the partition-content definition of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] to weak compositions, including internal zero counts; a zero count means that its label is absent. The set is finite, since at most $d^n$ fillings occur for $n>0$, and at $n=0$ its unique member is the empty filling.

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

Put $M:= igoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and define the **q-Schur algebra** $$S(d,n):=\mathrm{End}_H(M),$$ the $R$-algebra of right $H$-module endomorphisms of $M$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $F$ have characteristic $p>0$, let $N\ge2$, and let $\mu=(\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge\mu_N\ge0)$ be a polynomial highest weight. Let $L_N(\mu)$ be the nonzero Schur Weyl-cell simple at $q=1$, regarded as a left module by star, with its canonical highest vector $v$. Put $a_i=\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}$. For every $1\le r\le s<N$, define $B(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^j a_t$ and $C(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^{j-1}a_t$, reduced modulo $p$ for zero tests. A matching is an injection $d$ with $x\le d(x)$; it need not preserve order between different sources. Call $J\subseteq(r,s]$ essential when no $t<u$ outside $J$ in $[r,s+1]$ admits a zero-$B$ matching $\{t\}\cup(J\cap(t,u))\to[t,u)$. Write $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$ for the number of essential sets.

The vectors $T_{r,s}(J)v$ constructed by the explicit integral coefficient recursion in the proof, indexed by essential $J$, form a basis of $L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha_r-\cdots-\alpha_s}$. In particular this weight-space dimension is $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, including dimension zero. The construction has integer-polynomial coefficients, and its positive-word pivots remain valid in every field of characteristic $p$.

Define a root $x$ to be normal in $[x,y]$ when $a_x\ne0$ and its demands $m>x$ with $B(x,m)=0$ admit an injection $z$ satisfying $x<z(m)\le m$ and $B(z(m),m)=0$. If $r$ is not normal set $\nu_a(r,s)=0$; otherwise let it be the number of $x\in[r,s]$ normal in $[x,s]$ with $C(r,x)=0$. Set $\varepsilon'_a(r,t)=\varepsilon_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$, where only coordinate $t$ is increased by one. Then, as ordinary integers,
$$\varepsilon_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^s\varepsilon'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s).$$
No restrictedness condition is imposed on $\mu$ or on the shifted auxiliary highest weights.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $F$ be a
field of characteristic $p$. Let $\beta_F$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form on $M^\lambda_F=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, with
orthonormal tabloid basis, and let
$$S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad R^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F\cap(S^\lambda_F)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F/R^\lambda_F,$$
where $V^{\perp}=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]],
[[thm-james-submodule-theorem-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Let $G_\lambda$ be
the Gram matrix of the integral tabloid form in the standard-polytabloid
basis of the integral Specht lattice $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, and let
$g_\lambda$ be the positive greatest common divisor of its entries
([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]],
[[lem-specht-gram-gcd-detects-p-regularity]]). Write $G_\lambda\bmod p$ for
the entrywise image of $G_\lambda$ in $F$, a matrix with entries in $F$.
Then:

1. **Vanishing criterion.**
   $$D^\lambda_F=0\iff p\mid G_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j \iff p\mid g_\lambda\iff\lambda\text{ is not }p\text{-regular},$$
   and equivalently $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ if and only if $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for
   every $j\ge1$, where $z_j(\lambda)$ is the number of parts of $\lambda$
   equal to $j$.
2. **Dimension.** $\dim_FD^\lambda_F=\operatorname{rank}_F(G_\lambda\bmod p)$;
   this dimension is determined by $\lambda$ and $p$ alone, and it is
   positive exactly when $\lambda$ is $p$-regular.
3. **Structure when nonzero.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then
   $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ is the simple, self-dual and absolutely irreducible
   head of $S^\lambda_F$, and $R^\lambda_F$ is the unique maximal submodule
   of $S^\lambda_F$, equal to the module radical
   $\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_F)$.

For the $k$ of a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$,
$D^\lambda_k$ is the modular Specht quotient $D^\lambda$ of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], so the criterion above
decides for which $\lambda$ that quotient vanishes. No simplicity of
$S^\lambda_F$ itself is asserted.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Fix a prime $p$, an integer $n\ge0$, and a **splitting $p$-modular system**
$(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$, so that $K$ and $k$ are splitting fields for
$S_n$ and its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). Write

$$M^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad S^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\subseteq M^\lambda_k$$

for the base change of the integral tabloid module and Specht lattice; the
inclusion is the injective polytabloid-span inclusion of
[[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], and $S^\lambda_k$ has the
images of the standard polytabloids as $k$-basis. Let
$\beta_k:M^\lambda_k\times M^\lambda_k\to k$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form, the unique $k$-bilinear form with orthonormal tabloid basis
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]); it is
symmetric, nondegenerate, and $S_n$-invariant.

For a $k$-subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_k$ put

$$V^{\perp}:=\{\,x\in M^\lambda_k:\beta_k(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\,\}.$$

The **form radical** of $S^\lambda_k$ is

$$R^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k\cap (S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},$$

and the **modular Specht quotient** (or James quotient) is

$$D^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda .$$

The quotient is a $k[S_n]$-module and may be zero. Its dimension is the
$p$-rank of the integral Gram matrix: if $G_\lambda$ is the Gram matrix of
$\beta$ in the standard-polytabloid basis and $\overline{G_\lambda}$ its
reduction modulo $p$, i.e. the matrix of $\beta_k$ in the standard basis of
$S^\lambda_k$, then

$$\dim_kD^\lambda=\operatorname{rank}_k\overline{G_\lambda} =\operatorname{rank}_k(G_\lambda\bmod p).$$

Everything is defined by scalar extension: $S^\lambda_k$ and $\beta_k$ are
determined by $\lambda$ and $k$, and no choice of lifts of elements of
$S^\lambda_k$ enters. $R^\lambda$ is a **form radical**, and is an
$S_n$-submodule; the identification of $R^\lambda$ with the module radical
$\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)=J(k[S_n])S^\lambda_k$
([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]) is a later consequence,
asserted only when $D^\lambda\ne0$. In particular no simplicity of
$D^\lambda$ is claimed here.

In the notation of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]], let
$B$ be an addable $i$-node of the $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ such that
$\nu=\mu\cup B$ is again $p$-restricted, and let $F_i$ be the residue-summand
induction functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $B$ is not a conormal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B':\ B'\ \text{conormal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly above }B\}$$
(counting $B$ itself) if $B$ is conormal. The dual Specht-to-induction Hom
criterion (Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.7(i), Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5 dual
form) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].
