derivations.claim: We first establish the restriction endpoint locally. Work with left Schur modules through star. In tensor degree $m$, the word of $m_\alpha T_w$ has $j$th letter the row containing $j$ in $t^\alpha w$; at regular type it is $jw^{-1}$, with zero-multiplicity labels omitted. Over $K=F(t)$ the evaluations $g^{\otimes m}$ span the tensor Schur algebra: a functional killing them gives a polynomial zero on invertible matrices; multiplication by $\det$ and the infinite-field polynomial identity force that polynomial to be zero. Schur simples are therefore simple polynomial $\mathrm{GL}_N$ modules. The canonical shape/type diagonal is its permutation-summand projection, whose square gives canonical form value one. Semistandard column strictness bounds entries at most $k$ by the first $k$ rows, so all weights are dominated by the highest weight $\xi$ and the highest space is $Kv$. Integer torus characters, rather than Lie eigenvalues modulo $p$, distinguish these weights.

Gaussian factorization $g=u^-tu^+$ on the big cell shows that negative coefficient operators on $v$ span its simple module: a functional killing them kills $gv$ on that open set and hence everywhere by polynomial identity. Similarly, positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\xi-\Gamma$. If every positive highest coefficient vanished, the highest coefficient of $gx$ would vanish on the big cell, because negative operators cannot raise any weight to $\xi$; it would then vanish on the orbit of $x$, which spans the simple and contains $v$. All coefficient operators have integral tensor replacement matrices, and the ranks and Hom kernels of finite matrices preserve extension from $F$ to $K$. These arguments consequently descend to $F$.

Let $\xi_N=0$, $l=N-1$, and let $M$ be the full last-coordinate-one subspace of $L_N(\xi)$. A primitive vector means one killed by every nonconstant coefficient of the upper Levi unipotent group, not merely by its Lie generators. Factor the full upper group as $V U_l^+$, where $V$ has only the last column above the diagonal nontrivial. A positive test of a Levi-primitive vector acts only through $V$, since the right-hand nonconstant Levi coefficients kill it. Raising last coordinate $1$ to highest coordinate $0$ requires a $V$ monomial of degree exactly one. Positive detection therefore gives $E_{rN}x=cv\ne0$ for some $r$. Hence $\operatorname{wt}(x)=\xi-\beta_r$, where $\beta_r=\alpha_r+\cdots+\alpha_l$, even when the initial first-level deficit was arbitrary. On that primitive weight space $x\mapsto E_{rN}x$ is injective by the same detection argument, so its dimension is at most one.

Put $a_j=\xi_j-\xi_{j+1}$ and use $B(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^s a_j$ and $C(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^{s-1}a_j$. For nonempty $I$, the canonical $Q(I)$ kills a primitive vector: if $b=\min I$, its ascending-prefix letter $e_{b-1}$ commutes past the remaining ascending letters, whose indices exceed $b$, and becomes a rightmost Levi letter with $b-1<l$. Expand a nonzero primitive vector of weight $\xi-\beta_r$ in the essential $T$ basis and select the largest hat among its nonzero coefficients. The triangular pivot isolates a nonzero term. That hat cannot be nonempty, since its $Q$ test would annihilate the vector. Distinct essential hats therefore leave exactly one essential set with empty hat. Empty is linked precisely to a regular set, and the essential-regular matching theorem says such a set exists precisely when $r$ is normal. This proves necessity of normality.

Conversely, for normal $r$ let $R_r=\{s\in(r,l]:B(r,s)=0\}$ and choose its compensation $f$ with $r<f(s)\le s$ and $B(f(s),s)=0$. Put $D=f(R_r)$. The inverse matching makes $D$ regular, so its hat is empty. The matched norm is $\Xi_{r,l}(D)=\prod_{s\in[r,l]\setminus R_r}B(r,s)\ne0$: $B(r,r)=a_r\ne0$, and $R_r$ removes exactly the other zero factors. Thus $T_{r,l}(D)v$ is nonzero, and the maximal-hat assertion gives $h(I,D)=0$ for every nonempty $I$. For $r\le j<l$, every positive test of $e_jT(D)v$ has grade $\beta_r-\alpha_j$. Expanding its root matrices into simple words and appending the rightmost $e_j$ gives full words with nonempty canonical $Q$ index, since $e_j$ acts before $e_{j+1}$. All highest coefficients vanish, so positive detection gives $e_jT(D)v=0$. For $j<r$ the target weight is outside dominance below $\xi$ and is zero. A nonconstant Levi coefficient whose weight is not bounded by $\beta_r$ likewise has zero target. At a weight bounded by $\beta_r$, root-variable exponents are at most one, so the coefficient is a product of positive root matrices, each an iterated simple-root commutator; its rightmost root kills the vector. This proves full group primitivity. The primitive line at $\xi-\beta_r$ is consequently one-dimensional exactly at normal $r$, and we denote any nonzero vector on it by $v_r$.

We separate primitive labels integrally, including $p=2$. In tensor degree $b$ for Levi rank $l$, put $H_a=E_{aa}$ and define $\binom{H_a}{2}$ to act on a weight $\zeta$ by the integer $\binom{\zeta_a}{2}$ reduced in $F$. Concretely it is $\sum_{x<y}E_{aa}^{(x)}E_{aa}^{(y)}$, with no division by $2$ in $F$. The tensor action $Z_b$ of the group central transposition sum $z_b=\sum_{x<y}(x,y)$ satisfies the exact integer identity $Z_b=\sum_a\binom{H_a}{2}+\sum_{a<c}(E_{ac}E_{ca}-H_a)$. The equal-position part of $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ is $H_a$; after subtracting it, the terms are exactly the two swaps of unequal labels. The diagonal terms count equal-label pairs. Since $z_b$ commutes with the position group and every Schur endomorphism, this operator belongs to the Schur algebra and is central.

On a primitive vector of dominant weight $\zeta$, $E_{ac}$ kills it for $a<c$, so $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ acts by $H_a-H_c$. Therefore $Z_b$ has scalar $\kappa(\zeta)=\sum_a\binom{\zeta_a}{2}-\sum_c(c-1)\zeta_c=\sum_{(c,j)\in[\zeta]}(j-c)$. The binomial here is the actual diagonal weight operator of step 6.1. Centrality makes this scalar constant on the cyclic module generated by the vector. For first-level $\zeta_r=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_l)-\epsilon_r$, it is $\kappa(\zeta_r)=\kappa(\xi)- (\xi_r-r)$, so $\kappa(\zeta_t)-\kappa(\zeta_r)=-C(t,r)$. Thus the cyclic Levi module $\Psi_r$ generated by $v_r$ cannot contain another primitive $v_t$ when $C(t,r)\ne0$. Equality of the scalars alone does not prove simplicity; we treat it explicitly next.

Suppose $t<r$ are normal and $C(t,r)=0$. Choose $D$ for the demands of $r$ as in step 5.1. For $w\ge r$, $B(t,w)=B(r,w)$, and $B(t,r)=a_r
e0$. The demands of $t$ split into $Y=\{y\in(t,r):B(t,y)=0\}$ and $R_r$. Compensation for $Y$, inherited from normality of $t$, has image $E$ below $r$. Since $B(t,r-1)=C(t,r)-1=-1
e0$, all those targets and $E$ lie at most $r-2$. Combining their matching with $D$ gives compensation for every demand of $t$, so choose $v_t=T_{t,l}(E\cup D)v$ and $v_r=T_{r,l}(D)v$. For each $e\in E$ its matched $y$ gives $B(e,y)=B(t,y)=0$, hence $C(t,e)=0$. If $E
e\varnothing$ and $e=\max E$, then $C(e,r)=C(t,r)-C(t,e)=0$.

Splitting (P) gives $T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r=v_t-T_{t,l}((E\setminus\{e\})\cup\{r\}\cup D)v-C(e,r)T_{t,l}(E\cup\{r\}\cup D)v$. The last term is zero. The middle term has a (Z) witness with endpoint $r-1$, outside its cuts because $E\le r-2$ and $D>r$. Removing matched source $e$ releases its zero-$B$ target $y_e$; assign $t$ to $y_e$ and retain the matching on $E\setminus\{e\}$. All distinct bounded targets are below $r-1$. Hence that term is zero as well. For $E=\varnothing$, (P) omits the middle term and its last coefficient is $C(t,r)=0$. In both cases $v_t=T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r\in\Psi_r$, without a field denominator.

The Gaussian argument on a cyclic module, without assuming simplicity, shows that $\Psi_r$ is spanned by negative Levi coefficients on $v_r$ and has weights at most $\zeta_r$. Any nonzero proper Schur submodule contains a simple Schur submodule and thus a primitive $v_t$ by step 3.1. Dominance gives $t\le r$. For $t=r$, its one-dimensional line is the generating line and would generate all of $\Psi_r$; thus a proper submodule has $t<r$, and the central scalar requires $C(t,r)=0$. Conversely, such an earlier normal $t$ gives a proper nonzero $\Psi_t\subset\Psi_r$ by step 9.1, since its weights are at most $\zeta_t<\zeta_r$. Consequently $\Psi_r$ is simple precisely when $r$ is normal with no earlier normal $t$ satisfying $C(t,r)=0$. All simple Schur submodules of $M$ are exactly these $\Psi_r$, each once: every simple has a primitive highest vector, and each primitive line has dimension one.

Now assume $\xi$ restricted. The root criterion is its physical signature criterion: $a_r\ne0$ identifies the removable node in row $r$; scanning $j>r$, a nonzero $a_j$ gives a removable push if $C(r,j)=0$ and an addable pop at row $j+1$ if $B(r,j)=0$. These events have the residue of row $r$; at $a_j=0$ the matching slot supplies and consumes itself and is neutral. For $0<a_j<p$, the two events are disjoint. The compensation-prefix inequalities are exactly survival of the initial push in the signature stack. Also $C(t,r)=(\xi_t-t)-(\xi_r-r)$ compares the residues. Thus the simple cyclic modules in step 10.1 are exactly at the good nodes. Their lower labels are restricted: removing row $r$ decreases $a_r$ by one and increases $a_{r-1}$ by one. The only failure, when $r>1$, would be $a_{r-1}=p-1$. Then $C(r-1,r)=0$, and $r-1$ is also normal, since its later demands are those of $r$, $B(r-1,r)=a_r\ne0$, and the compensation for $r$ is also valid for $r-1$. This contradicts goodness. Hence every Schur socle factor survives the restricted-label corner; no assertion is made about the other composition factors.

To transfer without a held generic classifier, for $\xi\vdash m$ choose $N=m+1$ and the regular composition $\omega=(1^{m-1},0,1)$, so $\xi_N=0$ even for columns. Compute the cell corner temporarily in its original right-module convention, then transport through star. Its permutation summand is $M^\omega=FS_m$, and its actual projection $e$ gives $eSe=FS_m$ via $\rho_h(x)=hx$. Type-$\omega$ tableaux correspond to standard tableaux by increasing relabeling $1,\ldots,m-1,N$ to $1,\ldots,m$. Their normalized map fibers are singleton, and evaluation at $1$ sends $\varphi_{st}$ to $m_{st}$. Higher ideals correspond as equality of corner basis spans. The Weyl weight projection keeps exactly these basis vectors; read its cell action using a fixed outer index of the same type and evaluate at $1$ to get the Murphy action. Thus $W^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)$ with the actual same-shape normalization.

In the Schur cell product choose all four indices $a,s,t,b$ standard of type $\omega$. Evaluation at $1$ turns $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ into $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$, so the unique Murphy coefficient gives $B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)=G_\zeta(c_s,c_t)$. The factor is one. Since $e^*=e$, the Weyl splitting $W=We\oplus W(1-e)$ is orthogonal, giving $\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(We)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(W)e$, including zero corner forms. Projection is exact by lifting $ye$ through $xe$ and taking kernels fixed by $e$. Hence $L^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}$. The actual $q=1$ form-unit bridge identifies it with $D^{\zeta'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, nonzero exactly when $\zeta'$ is regular. Transporting these right-cell identities through star gives the corresponding left corners $eW^\zeta$ and $eL^\zeta$ used below. Their nonzero images are exactly the distinct absolutely simple restricted-label modules $D(\zeta)$, with the inverse group convention fixed by the nondegenerate quotient form.

Let $\pi_1$ be the sum of actual weight projections with last coordinate one, so $M=\pi_1L_N(\xi)$. The lower Schur orbit matrix $E_A$ embeds as $E_{\operatorname{diag}(A,1)}$; on each word with one $N$ it preserves that position and applies $E_A$ to the remaining ordered positions. Products agree and the lower identity is $\pi_1$, and transpose/star is respected. The lower regular projection of $\omega'=(1^{m-1},0)$ maps to $e$. On the coset-word convention of step 1.1, $\rho'_h$ acts by label permutation $h^{-1}$ on the used lower labels, fixing $N$, identically to $\rho_h$ for the subgroup fixing the last entry of $S_m$. Thus, in the left convention, $e'M=eL_N(\xi)\downarrow_{S_{m-1}}$. Write $S_L=S(N-1,m-1)$ for this lower Schur algebra; every socle and corner lift of $M$ below is over $S_L$. The inverse/star equivalence passes between right and left modules and commutes with this embedding, restriction and sign; the ordinary simple labels are fixed by their nondegenerate invariant quotient forms. No self-duality of a degenerate Specht module is assumed.

Socle preservation requires more than exactness. By step 11.1 every Schur socle simple of $M$ survives $e'$. A nonzero Schur submodule killed by $e'$ would contain a simple submodule inside that socle, whose corner is nonzero, a contradiction. Now a group-simple injection $j:D\to e'M$ corresponds to $S_Le'\otimes_{e'S_Le'}D\to M$, $se'\otimes x\mapsto sj(x)$, $s\in S_L$. Its image $I$ is generated by its corner $e'I=j(D)$. A proper Schur submodule $J$ of $I$ has either $e'J=0$, excluded by the no-killed-submodule property, or $e'J=e'I$, which generates $I$ and forces $J=I$. Thus $I$ is simple. Every group-simple corner submodule lifts to an actual Schur simple submodule, and conversely every surviving Schur simple has simple corner. Exactness on the semisimple sum, distinct labels and the one-dimensional primitive lines yield $\operatorname{soc}_{FS_{m-1}}(e'M)=e'\operatorname{soc}_{S_L} M$, multiplicity-free with exactly the good-deletion labels. The unused coordinate includes columns and $m=1$, whose lower degree-zero corner is $F$.

The group central $z_m$ acts on $D(\xi)$ by $\kappa(\xi)$, since its tensor action is step 6.1 and its regular-summand action is $\rho_{z_m}$; right multiplication equals left multiplication for this central element. On the good lower label it acts by $\kappa(\xi-A)$. Therefore $L_m=z_m-z_{m-1}$ has scalar $\operatorname{res}(A)$ on that simple submodule, with the restricted convention $c-r$. Primary projection selects just that residue, and socles respect the actual direct sum. We obtain $\operatorname{soc}E_iD(\xi)=D(\xi-A_i)$ when $\varepsilon_i(\xi)>0$, and zero otherwise. In the latter case $E_iD(\xi)=0$, since a nonzero finite-dimensional module contains a simple submodule.

The invariant nondegenerate quotient form makes $D(\xi)$ self-dual. A primary polynomial projector in $L_m$ is self-adjoint, since the inverse involution fixes $L_m$, so its summand has a restricted nondegenerate invariant form. Its head is therefore dual to its simple socle and is the same simple. Thus for every restricted $\eta,\tau$ of consecutive degrees, $\dim_F\operatorname{Hom}(E_iD(\eta),D(\tau))$ is one if $\varepsilon_i(\eta)>0$ and $\eta-\operatorname{good}_i(\eta)=\tau$, and zero otherwise. The scalar endomorphism ring is $F$ by absolute simplicity. This all-pairs criterion includes the zero case and all initially possible primitive weights; it does not discard middle composition factors.

We justify the needed functor interfaces locally. In $\mathbb ZS_n$ the Jucys identity is $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g$. Induct on $n$: choosing $u$ leaves $n$ fixed, and choosing $(a,n)$ inserts it next to $a$ in a cycle, bijectively covering the non-fixed permutations. Hence each elementary symmetric JM coefficient is central over every field. On a simultaneous primary tuple these operators have generalized eigenvalues equal to its elementary symmetric residue coefficients; nilpotence follows by expanding a polynomial in the commuting nilpotent differences. Distinct residue multisets have distinct coefficient tuples, since their monic products of prime-field linear factors retain multiplicities uniquely even in characteristic $p$. For each elementary symmetric operator, construct its univariate primary projectors by the same polynomial CRT construction as in [F5], then multiply these commuting projectors. This gives the content projector equal to the sum of tuple projectors of that content. This proves content centrality without factorial division, position-dependent symmetric-polynomial claims, or content-block primitivity. The projectors are inverse-fixed. For an input in content $\alpha$, induction projection by right $e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$ is the same as right $P_{d+1,i}$, because $ge_\alpha\otimes x=g\otimes e_\alpha x$. An absolutely simple $D(\mu)$ lies in exactly one of these central contents, since their scalar idempotents are orthogonal and sum to one; denote it by $\alpha$. Thus these interfaces agree with the actual functor definition.

Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $E_H:FG\to FH$ truncate group coefficients. For left modules the natural Frobenius map is $\Phi(g\otimes x)(y)=E_H(yg)x$, with coinduction action $(a q)(y)=q(ya)$. It is balanced and $G$-linear by $E_H(hz)=hE_H(z)$ and $E_H(zh)=E_H(z)h$. For a left-coset transversal $T$ of $G/H$, its inverse is $\Psi(q)=\sum_{r\in T}r\otimes q(r^{-1})$. The right cosets $Hr^{-1}$ partition $G$, so evaluation at $y$ has exactly the term $yr\in H$ and returns $q(y)$. On $g\otimes x$ the unique term with $r^{-1}g\in H$ balances back to $g\otimes x$. These verify both identities and naturality with correct cosets and only finite choices.

Let $e=e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$, commuting with $FH$ and inverse-fixed. For any such centralizer element, $E_H(eZ)=E_H(Ze)$: the coefficient at $h$ is the group coefficient trace $\tau(h^{-1}eZ)=\tau(h^{-1}Ze)$, by cyclicity and commuting $e$ with $h^{-1}$. $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]), the
operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most
one cogood node exist in each residue. No module-theoretic statement is made
here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.

transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Every $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$ is obtained from the empty partition by $d$ successive cogood
additions: there are residues $i_1,\dots,i_d$ with
$$\mu=\tilde f_{i_d}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing;$$
equivalently, every $p$-restricted $\mu\ne\varnothing$ has at least one good

join $\nu$ to $\tilde f_i\nu$ for every $i$ for which the operator is
defined, the empty partition is the unique vertex of rank $0$ and every
vertex is reached from it; dually every vertex reaches the empty partition by

Let $F$ be any field, $q\in F^\times$ have finite quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, and let $H_d=H_{F,q}(S_d)$ with $(T_j-q)(T_j+1)=0$. For additive Hecke JM elements $L_d$, let $E_i$ be the $[i]_q$-generalized eigenspace in restriction to $H_{d-1}$; let $F_i$ be induction followed by its commuting right $[i]_q$-primary projector. These functors are defined over $F$, for $i\in\mathbb Z/e$, with $[i]_1=i$ and $[i]_q=(q^i-1)/(q-1)$ otherwise.

For every restricted $\lambda$ the nonzero $E_iD(\lambda)$ have simple socle and simple head $D(\widetilde e_i\lambda)$, each once, and $E_iD(\lambda)=0$ exactly when the good $i$-deletion is undefined. Similarly the nonzero $F_iD(\mu)$ have simple socle and simple head $D(\widetilde f_i\mu)$, each once, and vanish exactly when the cogood $i$-addition is undefined. Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. derivations.claim: An integral symmetric polynomial evaluates in $\mathbb ZS_n$. Its commutator with any permutation vanishes in $\mathbb CS_n$ by [F1], hence vanishes integrally by coefficientwise injectivity. For any coefficient ring, invariance of a polynomial under variable permutations says exactly that its coefficients are constant on monomial orbits, so it is a linear combination of integral monomial symmetric polynomials. All their evaluations are therefore central over $R$. A group-ring element is central exactly when its coefficients are constant on conjugacy classes: compare coefficients after conjugating by each permutation. Consequently the class sums form a basis of the center over $\mathbb Z$ and over $R$, even with zero divisors.

Define the reduced cycle type $\rho(g)$ by subtracting one from each nontrivial cycle length and discarding fixed points. Its size $d(g)=n-c(g)$ is the minimum number of transpositions expressing $g$: multiplying by a transposition changes the number of cycles by one, giving the lower bound, and each cycle of length $s$ has a factorization with $s-1$ transpositions, giving equality. The possible types are precisely partitions $\rho$ with $|\rho|+\ell(\rho)\le n$. Write $K_\rho$ for their integral class sums.

If a word of $d$ transpositions has product of degree $d$, every prefix multiplication joins two different cycles; otherwise the final degree would be at most $d-2$. The graph whose edges are the transpositions is therefore a forest, and its connected components are exactly the cycles of every prefix product. Indeed initially both are singletons, and each multiplication joins two current components by one edge and joins their two cycles. Thus edges never repeat, and each final tree of $s$ vertices gives a cycle of length $s$.

Let $\rho$ be a possible reduced type of size $d$, and expand the monomial symmetric polynomial $m_\rho(L_1,\ldots,L_n)$, summing once over distinct assignments of the positive parts of $\rho$ to distinct indices $r$. Each term is a word of $d$ transpositions, grouped into stars centered at those $r$: the group $L_r^a$ has $a$ edges incident to $r$. Every resulting permutation has degree at most $d$. If its degree is $d$, step 2.1 makes all these stars trees with distinct edges. Each star lies in one final tree; the degree of that tree is the sum of the exponents of its stars. Its reduced cycle type is therefore obtained from $\rho$ by merging some parts. Any proper merging decreases the number of parts.

The coefficient at any permutation $g$ of reduced type exactly $\rho$ is one. In the degree-$d$ expansion, equality of the number of parts forces each final tree to contain exactly one star. For a cycle with support $\{r,a_1,\ldots,a_s\}$, the center of its star must be its largest letter $r$, since every factor from $L_r$ is $(a,r)$ with $a<r$. The ordered star factorization is unique: with right-to-left permutation composition, $(a_1,r)\cdots(a_s,r)$ is the cycle $(r,a_s,\ldots,a_1)$, as direct evaluation on each letter shows. Thus the cycle determines the leaf ordering. Different cycles have distinct maxima, their stars are disjoint and commute, and their assignments appear exactly once among the distinct monomials, including repeated exponents. This also constructs a term producing $g$.

By centrality and steps 3.1–4.1, $m_\rho(L)=K_\rho+\sum_\sigma a_{\rho\sigma}K_\sigma$, with integer coefficients, where every remaining type either has smaller degree or is a proper merging of $\rho$. Induct on degree and, within a degree, on the number of parts in increasing order. All remaining sums are already integral symmetric polynomial evaluations, so subtraction expresses $K_\rho$ that way too. The initial type is empty with $m_\varnothing=K_\varnothing=1$. This proves integral spanning without division. Specialization to $R$ and the class-sum basis from step 1.1 prove the assertion over every $R$, including $n=0$ and the zero ring.

For disjoint sets let $h=\min(A\cup B)$. If $h\in A$, multiply $H(A\setminus\{h\},B)$ by $x_h-x_i$. If $h\in B$, put $P=H(A,B\setminus\{h\})$; splitting the sum according to $h\in D$ gives $(P-P|_{x_i=x_h})/(x_h-x_i)$. Divided difference of $x_i^m$ is $-\sum_{a=0}^{m-1}x_i^ax_h^{m-1-a}$, so induction proves $H\in\mathbb Z[x]$ even at coincident coordinates. Also $H(\varnothing,B)=\delta_{B,\varnothing}$ by the same recursion. For $k\in A$, $h=\max([i,k)\setminus A)$, splitting $x_k-x_{p_D(k)}=(x_k-x_h)+(x_h-x_{p_D(k)})$ gives $$H(A,B)=(x_k-x_h)H(A\setminus\{k\},B)+\mathbf1_{h\ne i}H((A\setminus\{k\})\cup\{h\},B)+\mathbf1_{k\in B}H_{i,k}(A\cap(i,k),B\cap(i,k))H_{k,j}(A\cap(k,j),B\cap(k,j)).$$ Indeed $(h,k)\subseteq A$, so common factors there first cancel. The second difference is zero when $h\in D$; otherwise its predecessor equals $p_D(h)$, giving the second term. The extra $k\in D$ terms have negative sign and split independently at $k$, giving the positive third product after subtraction. This accounts for every summand.

Put $C=I\setminus A$ and $$K(A)=\sum_{B\subseteq I}H(A,B)\prod_{t\in\{i\}\cup B}(y_{t+1}-x_t).$$ Expansion of each $y_{t+1}-x_{p_D(t+1)}$ as $(y_{t+1}-x_t)+(x_t-x_{p_D(t+1)})$ gives $$K(A)=\sum_{D\subseteq C}(-1)^{|D|}\frac{\prod_{t=i}^{j-1}(y_{t+1}-x_{p_D(t+1)})}{\prod_{t\in C}(x_t-x_{p_D(t)})}.$$ Selected difference factors vanish when their index belongs to $D$; the remaining predecessor is $p_D(t)$, and collection gives exactly $H(A,B)$ by cancellation of the complement numerator/denominator sets. For a bijection $\theta:C\to B_0\subseteq I$ with $\theta(c)\ge c$, this implies the matched-product identity $$K(A)\equiv\prod_{t\in[i,j)\setminus B_0}(y_{t+1}-x_i)\pmod{(y_{\theta(c)+1}-x_c:c\in C)}.$$ Here is an integral induction proof. If $C=\varnothing$, the alternating expression is the asserted full product. Otherwise take $h=\min C$, remove its source and target, and apply induction on $(h,j)$. Splitting the alternating sum by $h\in D$ gives the prefix product times the divided difference of $K_{h,j}$ in $x_h$. The prefix is $\prod_{t=i}^{h-1}(y_{t+1}-x_i)$ and the divided difference is $(K_{h,j}|_{x_h=x_i}-K_{h,j})/(x_h-x_i)$. All remaining match generators are independent of $x_h$, so divided differencing retains their ideal. The induction product contains the target $\theta(h)$; modulo its match it vanishes before substitution, and after substitution its factor is $x_h-x_i$. Cancel that integral factor to leave exactly the tail product with this target removed. No target occurs below $h$, since targets are at least their sources. The prefix completes the stated product. All divisions here are polynomial divided differences, not evaluation of rational functions.

The matching criterion is exactly the signature criterion. A zero $c_{i,k}$ records a later removable push of the same residue and a zero $b_{i,k}$ a later addable pop; nonremovable equal rows have both slots and cancel as a neutral pair. Removing common demand/support slots preserves the prefix inequalities for $B\downarrow C$. The remaining prefix inequalities say that the minus at row $i$ survives all later pops. Thus matched rows are normal, and the first matched row of a residue is its good row. Good deletion preserves restrictedness: its only possible new gap $e$ is above the deleted row, when $\lambda_{i-1}-\lambda_i=e-1$. The adjacent removable corners then have the same residue and no intervening same-residue boundary corner; if the lower minus survives, the upper minus survives too, contradicting first-surviving selection. The dual adjacent-plus argument proves cogood addition preserves restrictedness. Flipping the selected minus to plus changes no other $i$-boundary status, since all other changed corners have residues $i\pm1$, different from $i$ even at $e=2$. Before the first surviving minus the stack is empty, and every suffix prefix has at least as many remaining minus pushes as plus pops; after the flip these are exactly the conditions for the last surviving plus. Hence good deletion and cogood addition are inverse partial moves on restricted partitions.

Ordinary tensor adjunction and this Frobenius adjunction therefore give both $\operatorname{Hom}_B(F_iX,Y)=\operatorname{Hom}_H(X,E_iY)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_B(Y,F_iX)=\operatorname{Hom}_H(E_iY,X)$.
